answer: Manual pumps are cheaper but may not be as quick as an electric pump. Electric pumps may be stronger and allow for more milk to be expressed in less time. The suction strength can be altered on some electric pumps.

question: How can someone store breast milk?
answer: Breast milk can be stored in a sterilised container or special breast milk storage bags in the fridge for up to 8 days at 4C or lower, for 2 weeks in the ice compartment of a fridge, or for up to 6 months in a freezer if it's -18C or lower.

question: What is the best way to defrost frozen breast milk?
answer: It's best to defrost frozen breast milk slowly in the fridge before giving it to your baby. If you need to use it straight away, you can defrost it by putting it in a jug of warm water or holding it under running warm water. Once it's defrosted, give it a gentle shake if it has separated. Use it straight away. Do not re-freeze milk that's been defrosted.

question: What is the recommended method to warm up breast milk?
answer: You can warm up breast milk by putting the bottle in a jug of warm water or holding it under running warm water. Do not use a microwave to heat up or defrost breast milk. This can cause hot spots, which can burn your baby's mouth.

question: How long can expressed milk be kept in a cool bag with ice packs?
answer: Breast milk that's been cooled in the fridge can be carried in a cool bag with ice packs for up to 24 hours.

question: What should someone do if they're having difficulty expressing breast milk?
answer: If you're finding it difficult or uncomfortable to express your breast milk, you should ask your midwife, health visitor, or breastfeeding supporter for help. They can also tell you about other breastfeeding support available near you. You can search online for breastfeeding support in your area or call the National Breastfeeding Helpline on 0300 100 0212 (9.30am to 9.30pm daily).

question: How can I prepare for breastfeeding before the birth?
answer: It's good to find out as much as you can about breastfeeding before you have your baby. Antenatal classes usually cover the most important aspects of breastfeeding, such as positioning and attachment, expressing, and how to tackle common breastfeeding problems. You can also find out about breastfeeding from your midwife, family and friends, and useful helplines and websites. There are lots of groups and drop-ins, some specially designed for pregnant women who want to know more about breastfeeding.

question: What is skin-to-skin contact and why is it important?
answer: Skin-to-skin contact means holding your baby naked or dressed only in a nappy against your skin, usually under your top or under a blanket. Having skin-to-skin contact with your baby straight after giving birth will help to keep them warm and calm and steady their breathing. It is a great time to have your first breastfeed, and it also helps your baby attach to your breast using their natural crawling and latching-on reflexes. It is a bonding experience for both you and your baby, and it can also help to comfort you and your baby over the first few days and weeks as you get to know each other.

question: What is colostrum and why is it important for the baby?
answer: The fluid your breasts produce in the first few days after birth is called colostrum. It's thick and usually a golden yellow colour. It's a very concentrated food, so your baby will only need a small amount, about a teaspoonful, at each feed. Your baby may want to feed quite often, perhaps every hour to begin with. They'll begin to have fewer, but longer feeds once your breasts start to produce more "mature" milk after a few days. Colostrum is important for the baby because it is rich in antibodies and other immune-boosting nutrients which help to protect the baby from infections and illnesses.

question: What is the let-down reflex and how does it work?
answer: Your baby's sucking causes muscles in your breasts to squeeze milk towards your nipples. This is called the let-down reflex. Some women get a tingling feeling, which can be quite strong. Others feel nothing at all. You'll see your baby respond when your milk lets down. Their quick sucks will change to deep rhythmic swallows as the milk begins to flow. Babies often pause after the initial quick sucks while they wait for more milk to be delivered. Occasionally this let-down reflex can be so strong that your baby coughs and splutters.

question: How often should I feed my baby in the first week?
answer: In the first week, your baby may want to feed very often. It could be every hour in the first few days. Feed your baby as often as they want and for as long as they want. They'll begin to have fewer, but longer feeds after a few days. As a very rough guide, your baby should feed at least 8 to 12 times, or more, every 24 hours during the first few weeks.

question: How can I build up my milk supply?
answer: Around 2 to 4 days after birth you may notice that your breasts become fuller. This is often referred to as your milk "coming in". Each time your baby feeds, your body knows to make more milk for the next feed. The amount of milk you make will increase or decrease depending on how often your baby feeds. It is important to breastfeed at night because this is when you produce more hormones (prolactin) to build up your milk supply. In the early weeks, before you and your baby have become comfortable with breastfeeding, "topping up" with formula milk or giving your baby a dummy can lower your milk supply.

question: What should I do if I am having difficulties with breastfeeding?
answer: Ask a midwife or health visitor for help. They can also tell you about other breastfeeding support available near you. You can search online for breastfeeding support in your area or call the National Breastfeeding Helpline on 0300 100 0212 (9.30am to 9.30pm daily). You can find out about positioning and attachment, including how to get comfortable and make sure your baby is properly attached. If you are having difficulties with breastfeeding, take a look at common breastfeeding problems.

question: Is it possible to overfeed a breastfed baby?
answer: No, it is not possible to overfeed a breastfed baby. Feed your baby as often as they want and for as long as they want. They'll begin to have fewer, but longer feeds after a few days as they get used to breastfeeding. When your baby is hungry, they may show early feeding cues such as getting restless, sucking their fist or fingers, making murmuring sounds, or turning their head and opening their mouth (rooting). It's best to try and feed your baby during these early feeding cues as a crying baby is difficult to feed.

question: What should I do if my breasts are leaking milk unexpectedly?
answer: Wearing breast pads will stop your clothes becoming wet with breast milk. Remember to change them frequently to prevent an infection. Expressing some milk may also help. Only express enough to feel comfortable as you do not want to overstimulate your supply. If your baby has not fed recently, you could offer them a feed as breastfeeding is also about you being comfortable.

question: What is responsive feeding and why is it important?
answer: Responsive feeding is feeding your baby as often as they want and for as long as they want, responding to your baby's needs. It's also known as on-demand or baby-led feeding. Feed your baby when they show early feeding cues such as getting restless, sucking their fist or fingers, making murmuring sounds, or turning their head and opening their mouth (rooting). In the beginning, it can feel like you're doing nothing but feeding. But gradually you and your baby will get into a pattern and the amount of milk you produce will settle down. It's important to breastfeed at night because this is when you produce more hormones (prolactin) to build up your milk supply.

question: How often should I breastfeed my baby?
answer: Your baby should be breastfed at least 8 times every 24 hours during the first few weeks. However, every mother and baby are different, and you and your baby will work out your own feeding pattern together. You should not hesitate to feed your baby whenever they're hungry or need comfort.

question: How long should each breastfeeding session last?
answer: There is no exact duration for each breastfeeding session. Some babies prefer to feed for longer periods, while others prefer frequent short feeds, or a mixture of both. It's advisable to offer your baby the second breast after they have finished the first. If you are worried about your baby's feeding pattern or have concerns about breastfeeding, speak to a midwife or a breastfeeding specialist.

question: For how long should I breastfeed my baby?
answer: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months is recommended, followed by breastfeeding alongside solid foods. You and your baby can continue to enjoy the benefits of breastfeeding for as long as you want. Breastfeeding into your baby's second year or beyond, alongside other foods, is ideal. If you are going back to work or college, you can continue breastfeeding. Additionally, you do not have to stop breastfeeding if you get pregnant again.

question: What is responsive feeding and why is it important?
answer: Responsive feeding or "baby-led" or "on-demand" feeding means responding to your baby's cues. This not only ensures that the baby is getting enough milk, but also feeds them for comfort and reassurance. Newborn babies have a stomach the size of a walnut and need to feed little and often. Allowing babies to feed when they need to, will ensure that they're content and getting the milk they need, when they need it. It also stimulates your milk supply. Responsive feeding is essential for both you and the baby.

question: Can I breastfeed after a caesarean?
answer: Yes, you can. Immediately after the surgery, you should have a skin-to-skin cuddle with your baby. A midwife may help you have a skin-to-skin cuddle while you are in theatre or recovery. By keeping your baby close to you and having skin-to-skin contact, you may put them to your breast repeatedly, which helps in stimulating your milk supply. Rugby hold may be preferable for you, especially if you are experiencing pain due to the surgery. If you need pain relief, you can speak to a midwife.

question: Are there any reasons why I should not breastfeed?
answer: In rare cases, where there are sound medical reasons, breastfeeding may not be recommended. Examples include cases where the mother has HIV or is taking medication that can adversely affect the baby, such as some drugs for treating cancer. If you're not sure whether you should breastfeed your baby, you can always speak to a midwife or health visitor for information and support.

question: Can I still breastfeed even after having more than one baby?
answer: Yes, it's entirely possible to breastfeed twins, triplets, or other multiples. Breast milk is especially important for these babies because they are more likely to be born prematurely or have a low birthweight. You may find it easier to feed each of your babies separately when you start breastfeeding. Once you're confident, you can feed them at the same time. It's a good idea to talk to other mothers who have breastfed twins or more for support and advice.

question: Why can't I overfeed a breastfed baby?
answer: Breast milk has the right balance of nutrients and energy that your baby needs for growth and development. Your baby will instruct their body when they are hungry or full, and once they've had enough, they will stop taking milk. It, therefore, means that you cannot overfeed a breastfed baby, and so you should never hesitate to breastfeed when either of you wants to.

question: How can I get breastfeeding help and support?
answer: Breastfeeding can sometimes be a challenging experience, but there is help and support available. You can talk to a family member or friend who has experience with breastfeeding, or a GP, midwife, or health visitor, or call a helpline such as the National Breastfeeding Helpline. Additionally, you can look at reliable websites like The Breastfeeding Network, or your local breastfeeding support group, ask your health visitor for details.

question: Is there a correlation between responsive feeding and milk supply?
answer: Yes, there is. By allowing babies to feed when they need to, you stimulate your milk supply, which is crucial for milk production. The more you breastfeed, the more milk you'll produce because breastfeeding works on a supply-and-demand basis. Also, by responding to your baby's cues, you'll ensure that they're getting enough milk, even if that means feeding them more often than recommended.

question: How can I get my baby used to night and day?
answer: To teach your baby that night-time is different from daytime, try keeping the lights down low, not talking much and keeping your voice quiet, putting your baby down as soon as they've been fed and changed, not changing your baby unless they need it, and not playing with your baby. Your baby will gradually learn that night-time is for sleeping.

question: Where should my baby sleep?
answer: For the first 6 months, your baby should be in the same room as you when they're asleep, both day and night. This can reduce the risk of SIDS (sudden infant death syndrome). You can start getting your baby used to going to sleep without you comforting them by putting them down before they fall asleep or when they've just finished a feed.

question: What is SIDS?
answer: SIDS stands for sudden infant death syndrome, which is the sudden, unexplained death of a baby under 1 year of age, often during sleep. It's also known as "cot death".

question: How much sleep does a newborn baby need?
answer: Most newborn babies are asleep more than they are awake. Their total daily sleep varies, but can be from 8 hours up to 16 or 18 hours. Babies will wake during the night because they need to be fed. Being too hot or too cold can also disturb their sleep.

question: Should I change my baby during the night?
answer: You should only change your baby during the night if they need it, as unnecessary changes can disturb their sleep. If your baby's nappy leaks or if they have soiled it, you should change it as soon as possible. Otherwise, it's best to wait until the morning to change them.

question: When should I establish a bedtime routine for my baby?
answer: You may feel ready to introduce a bedtime routine when your baby is around 3 months old. Getting them into a simple, soothing bedtime routine can be a great opportunity to have 1-to-1 time with your baby.

question: How much sleep does a 2-year-old need?
answer: Most 2-year-olds will sleep for 11 to 12 hours at night, with 1 or 2 naps in the daytime.

question: What can I do if my baby is having problems sleeping?
answer: If your baby is having problems sleeping or you need more advice about getting into a routine, speak to your health visitor. All babies change their sleep patterns. Just when you think you have it sorted and you've all had a good night's sleep, the next night you might be up every 2 hours. Be prepared to change routines as your baby grows and enters different stages. Growth spurts, teething, and illnesses can all affect how your baby sleeps.

question: What should my baby wear to bed?
answer: You should dress your baby appropriately for the room temperature. In general, your baby should be dressed in no more than one extra layer than you would wear to be comfortable in the same room. Use a baby sleeping bag or light sheet to keep them warm, rather than blankets, which can cover their face and increase the risk of SIDS (sudden infant death syndrome).

question: What should I do if I'm not sleeping at the same time as my baby?
answer: If you're not sleeping at the same time as your baby, don't worry about keeping the house silent while they sleep. It's good to get your baby used to sleeping through a certain amount of noise. However, try to sleep when your baby sleeps, especially in the early weeks.

question: What is CPR?
answer: CPR stands for cardiopulmonary resuscitation, which is a life-saving procedure used in emergencies when someone's breathing or heartbeat has stopped.

question: What should I do if a child is unresponsive and not breathing normally?
answer: If a baby or child is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call 999 and start CPR straight away. When you call 999 for an ambulance, you should be given basic life-saving instructions over the phone, including advice about CPR.

question: What should I do if I think there has been an injury to the neck of the child?
answer: If you think there may have been an injury to the neck, tilt the head carefully, a small amount at a time, until the airway is open. Opening the airway takes priority over a possible neck injury.

question: What should I do if my child is breathing normally?
answer: If your child is breathing normally, turn them on their side, check for continued breathing, and send or go for help – do not leave your child unless absolutely necessary.

question: What are the steps for providing rescue breaths for a baby under 1 year?
answer: To give rescue breaths for a baby under 1 year, ensure the head is in a neutral position and lift the chin. Take a breath, then cover your baby's mouth and nose with your mouth, making sure it's sealed. If you cannot cover both the mouth and nose at the same time, just seal either with your mouth. If you choose the nose, close the lips to stop air escaping. Blow a breath steadily into the baby's mouth and nose over 1 second. It should be sufficient to make the chest visibly rise. Keeping their head tilted and chin lifted, take your mouth away and watch for the chest to fall as air comes out. Take another breath and repeat this sequence 4 more times.

question: What should I do if my child does not respond after I say: "Are you alright?"?
answer: If your child does not respond after you say, "Are you alright?"m, call for help. Carefully turn the child on their back. Then, follow the steps for checking their breathing and providing rescue breaths and chest compressions as necessary.

question: What should I do if my child is not breathing or is breathing infrequently and irregularly?
answer: If your child is not breathing or is breathing infrequently and irregularly, carefully remove any obvious obstruction in the mouth. Give 5 initial rescue breaths (mouth-to-mouth resuscitation). While doing this, note any gag or cough response – this is a sign of life. Then, follow the steps for performing CPR, including rescue breaths and chest compressions.

question: What is the rate of compressions for chest compressions?
answer: The rate of compressions for chest compressions is about 100-120 a minute, and after 30 compressions, tilt the head, lift the chin, and give 2 effective breaths. Continue compressions and breaths in a ratio of 2 breaths for every 30 compressions.

question: What should I do if I have difficulty achieving effective breathing in my child?
answer: If you have difficulty achieving effective breathing in your child, the airway may be obstructed. Open the child's mouth and remove any visible obstruction. Do not poke your fingers or any object into the mouth. Ensure there's adequate head tilt and chin lift, but the neck is not overextended. Make up to 5 attempts to achieve effective breaths (enough to make the chest visibly rise). If this is still unsuccessful, move on to chest compressions combined with rescue breaths.

question: When should I stop resuscitation?
answer: You should stop resuscitation if your child shows signs of life – normal breathing, coughing, movement of arms or legs, or qualified help arrives. Otherwise, you should continue resuscitation until further help arrives or your child begins to breathe normally for themselves.

question: What age range of children are more prone to choking?
answer: Children aged 1 to 5 years are more prone to choking as they tend to put small objects such as marbles, beads, and button batteries in their mouth.

question: What is the best way to avoid choking in children?
answer: Keeping small objects like marbles, beads, and button batteries out of your child's reach is the best way to avoid choking.

question: What should you do if your child starts choking?
answer: If your child suddenly starts coughing, isn't ill, and has a habit of putting small objects in their mouth, encourage them to carry on coughing to bring up what they're choking on. If coughing loudly doesn't work, try using back blows if your child is still conscious.

question: What should you do if you cannot see the object causing choking?
answer: If you cannot see the object causing choking, do not poke blindly or repeatedly with your fingers, as this could make matters worse by pushing the object further in and making it harder to remove.

question: How can you perform back blows on a baby under 1 year old?
answer: To perform back blows on a baby under 1 year old, sit down and lay your baby face down along your thigh or forearm, supporting their back and head with your hand, then give up to 5 sharp back blows with the heel of 1 hand in the middle of the back between the shoulder blades.

question: What can chest or abdominal thrusts do in case of choking?
answer: Chest or abdominal thrusts create an artificial cough, increasing pressure in the chest and helping to dislodge the object causing choking.

question: What can happen even if the object causing choking has come out?
answer: Even if the object causing choking has come out, medical help should be sought as part of the object might have been left behind or your child might have been hurt by the procedure.

question: What should you do if a choking child becomes unconscious?
answer: If a choking child becomes unconscious, shout for help, put them on a firm, flat surface, and call 999 while putting the phone on speakerphone so your hands are free. Open the child's mouth and remove the object if it is clearly visible and can be easily grasped. Start CPR and await help.

question: How many chest thrusts should be given to a baby under 1 year old?
answer: To give chest thrusts to a baby under 1 year old, find the breastbone and place 2 fingers in the middle, then give 5 sharp chest thrusts by compressing the chest by about a third.

question: What should you do if back blows and chest or abdominal thrusts do not work in dislodging the object causing choking?
answer: If back blows and chest or abdominal thrusts do not work in dislodging the object causing choking, call 999 and keep trying this cycle until help arrives. Also, seek medical help even if the object has come out as part of the object might have been left behind, or your child might have been hurt by the procedure.

question: What should I do if my child has an accident?
answer: Start by learning some basic first aid or revise what you already know. If you're worried about your child, call NHS 111. Use the guidelines discussed in the context to determine when to call an ambulance or when to take your child to A&E.

question: What should I do if my child is struggling for breath?
answer: You should immediately call an ambulance if your child is struggling for breath, breathing fast, panting, becoming very wheezy, or you see the muscles just under their ribcage sucking in when they breathe in.

question: What should I do if my child has a cut that will not stop bleeding?
answer: You should call an ambulance if your child has a cut that will not stop bleeding or is gaping open. Do not tie anything around the injury so tightly that it stops the circulation.

question: What should I do it my child has something lodged in their nose or ears?
answer: If your child has something lodged firmly in their nose or ear, leave it where it is. You may push it further in if you try to remove it. Take your child to the nearest A&E department or minor injuries unit. If their nose is blocked, show your child how to breathe through their mouth.

question: What should I do if my child swallows a button battery?
answer: If your child swallows a button battery, take them to A&E straight away. Button batteries are small round, silver batteries found in lots of electrical toys and devices. As well as being a choking hazard, button batteries can cause internal burns, internal bleeding, and sometimes death.

question: What should I do if my child has a burn or a scald?
answer: Immediately put the burn or scald under cool running water for 20 to 30 minutes, to reduce the heat in the skin. If there's no running water, immerse the burn or scald in cold water or use any other cool fluid, such as milk or another cold drink. Do not put butter, toothpaste, oil or ointment on a burn or scald. Depending on the severity of the burn or scald, see your GP or go to a minor injuries unit or A&E.

question: What should I do if I think my child has a broken bone?
answer: If you think your child's neck or spine may be injured, call an ambulance. Do not move them. Unnecessary movement could cause paralysis. If you cannot easily move your child without causing pain, call an ambulance. Comfort your child and take them to the hospital.

question: What should I do if my child feels unwell or faint after an accident?
answer: If your child looks pale or feels unwell after an accident, lie them down. Keep them covered up and warm, but not too hot. If your child feels faint, get them to keep their head down or, ideally, lie down. The faint feeling should wear off in a minute or two.

question: What should I do if my child has a cut and there's an object embedded in the wound?
answer: If there's an object embedded in the wound, like a piece of glass, press around the edges of the object, rather than directly on it. If you think there may be something in the cut, such as a piece of glass, go to A&E.

question: What should I do if I'm unsure if I should move my child after an accident?
answer: If you're unsure whether you should move your child, make sure they're warm and call an ambulance.

question: When should I buy a baby car seat?
answer: It's recommended to buy a baby car seat before your baby is born if possible.

question: What should I consider when buying a baby car seat?
answer: It's important to buy a seat that fits your car and is suitable for a newborn. Always choose a baby or child car seat that's right for your child's current height and weight. Think about how you will be using the car seat.

question: Should I try the car seat before buying?
answer: Yes, it's best to try a few car seats in your car before making a decision. Find a retailer who is willing to help you with this.

question: What is an i-Size car seat?
answer: i-Size is a European safety standard for baby and child car seats. It's part of regulation ECE R129, which will eventually replace the old safety regulation R44/04. Your car must have Isofix connectors for you to be able to use an i-Size car seat.

question: What are Isofix connectors?
answer: Isofix connectors are designed to make fitting baby and child car seats simpler. Most modern family cars have them. They may be hidden in the cracks between the padding of your car seats.

question: Should I buy a secondhand car seat?
answer: No, it is not recommended to buy a secondhand car seat as it could have been damaged in an accident, and may not have all its parts, including the instructions. It may also not be a user-friendly model and may not fit your car properly.

question: What size car seat should I get for my child?
answer: Car seats are divided into three main groups, depending on your baby or child's age and weight: group 0+ for babies up to 15 months or 13kg, group 1 for children who weigh 9-18kg or who are aged from 9 months to 4 years, and group 2/3 for children who weigh 15-36kg or are aged from 4 to 11 years. You can also buy combination seats that cross over these groups.

question: Can I use a rear-facing baby seat in a front passenger seat with an active airbag?
answer: No, it is dangerous and illegal to carry a baby in a rear-facing baby seat in a front passenger seat that has an active airbag.

question: How can I ensure my baby is safe in their car seat?
answer: Make sure your baby is securely strapped into the car seat according to the manufacturer's instructions. Always put your baby into their car seat from the pavement side of the car.

question: Where can I find additional help and advice on baby car seats?
answer: You can get advice from a good car seat retailer, the manufacturer, the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents (RoSPA) child car seats website, and the road safety officer at your local council. Additionally, GOV.UK provides information about baby car seats and the law.

question: What are the health risks for babies during hot weather?
answer: Babies and young children can become ill during very hot weather. Their health can be seriously affected by dehydration, heat exhaustion, heatstroke, and sunburn.

question: How can I protect my baby from the sun?
answer: Keep your baby cool and protect them from the sun. Babies less than 6 months old should be kept out of direct sunlight. Older babies should also be kept out of the sun as much as possible, particularly in the summer and between 11am and 3pm, when the sun is at its strongest. Apply a sunscreen with an SPF of at least 30 to your baby's skin, and make sure they wear a sunhat with a wide brim or a long flap at the back to protect their head and neck from the sun.

question: What kind of sunscreen should I use for my baby?
answer: Apply a sunscreen with an SPF of at least 30 to your baby's skin. Make sure the product also protects against both UVA and UVB rays. Many brands produce sunscreen specifically for babies and young children, as these products are less likely to contain additives that might irritate the skin.

question: How often should I apply sunscreen to my baby?
answer: Apply the suncream regularly, particularly if your child is in and out of the sea or paddling pool.

question: When should I keep my child out of the sun?
answer: Older babies should be kept out of the sun as much as possible, particularly in the summer and between 11am and 3pm, when the sun is at its strongest.

question: What drinks should I give to my baby during hot weather?
answer: Like adults, babies and young children need to drink plenty of fluids to avoid becoming dehydrated. Fully breastfed babies do not need any water until they've started eating solid foods. During hot weather, they may want to breastfeed more than usual. Once you have started to introduce solid foods, you should offer your baby sips of water from a cup or beaker with meals. Remember that breastmilk or infant formula should be their main drinks during the first year.

question: What can I do to keep my child cool during hot weather?
answer: Playing in a paddling pool is a good way of keeping babies and children cool. Keep the pool in the shade during very hot weather and supervise the children carefully at all times. Run them a cool bath before bedtime. Keep your child's bedroom cool during the day by closing blinds or curtains. You can also use a fan to circulate the air in the room. Keep nightwear and bedclothes to a minimum.

question: What drinks should I avoid giving to children under five years old?
answer: Undiluted fruit juice or smoothies should not be given to children until they are 5 years old as these can cause tooth decay.

question: What temperature should my baby's room be?
answer: A nursery thermometer will help you monitor the temperature of your baby's room. Your baby will sleep most comfortably when their room is between 16C and 20C.

question: Can I give my child frozen lollies during hot weather?
answer: In hot weather, you can try giving your child frozen lollies made from plain water or from very diluted fruit juice to help keep them hydrated. Lollies made from diluted fruit juice should only be given at mealtimes because they can cause tooth decay.

question: What temperature is considered normal for babies and children?
answer: A normal temperature in babies and children is about 36.4C, but this can vary slightly.

question: What body parts should I touch to determine if my baby has a high temperature?
answer: Your baby may have a high temperature if they feel hotter than usual to touch on their forehead, back, or stomach.

question: How do I know if my baby has a high temperature?
answer: Your baby may have a high temperature if they feel sweaty or clammy, and have flushed cheeks. It's best to check their temperature with a thermometer to see whether you need to get medical advice.

question: What is the most accurate way to take my baby's temperature?
answer: You need a digital thermometer to get a fast, accurate reading. You can buy these online or from pharmacies and most large supermarkets. To take your child's temperature, put the thermometer in their armpit and gently, but firmly hold their arm against their body.

question: What should I do if my child has been wrapped tightly in a blanket before taking their temperature?
answer: If your child has been wrapped up tightly in a blanket, allow them to cool down for a few minutes but do not let them get cold or shivery. Take their temperature again to see if there's any change.

question: Why shouldn't I use an old-fashioned glass thermometer?
answer: You should never use an old-fashioned glass thermometer containing mercury. They can break, releasing small splinters of glass and highly poisonous mercury. They're no longer used in hospitals and you cannot buy them in shops.

question: What causes a high temperature in children?
answer: A high temperature is usually a sign that your child's body is trying to fight an infection.

question: When should I contact a GP or call 111 if my child has a high temperature?
answer: You should contact a GP or call 111 if your child has other signs of illness, such as a rash, as well as a high temperature, or if your baby's temperature is 38C or higher if they're under 3 months old, or 39C or higher if they're 3 to 6 months old.

question: What should I do if my baby has a high temperature?
answer: Make sure you give them plenty of drinks to avoid dehydration. If you're breastfeeding, offer your baby plenty of feeds. You can usually look after your baby or child at home when they have a high temperature. Contact a GP or call 111 if you're concerned.

question: Can strip-type thermometers accurately take my child's temperature?
answer: No, strip-type thermometers are not an accurate way of taking a temperature. They show the temperature of the skin, rather than the body.

question: What is the purpose of collecting blood samples from newborns?
answer: Blood is collected from almost all newborn babies in the UK and stored on blood spot cards. The main purpose of this collection is for screening rare but serious conditions, to monitor the screening program, to investigate the cause of a baby's death, to provide information about diseases in families and to help us learn more about genetic conditions.

question: What is the newborn blood spot screening programme?
answer: Newborn blood spot screening program is an NHS program where spots of blood are collected from babies using a heel prick test. These blood spots are tested to find whether the baby has any of the nine rare but serious conditions. If a baby tests positive, they can be treated early, which can improve their health and prevent severe disability or even death.

question: How are stored blood spot cards used to investigate the cause of a baby's death?
answer: If the cause of a baby's death is unclear, doctors may request that the baby's stored blood spots be tested to find out the cause of death. This is done to determine whether the baby had a genetic condition that may have caused their death.

question: What information can be obtained from a baby's blood spot?
answer: A baby's blood spot can provide information about the mother's health, such as whether or not she has HIV. It can also provide information about genetic conditions that were present at birth or run in the family.

question: Can testing the blood spot cards provide information about parents' risk of having another baby with a certain condition in the future?
answer: In some cases, testing the stored blood spots of a previous baby may provide information about parents' risk of having another baby with a certain condition in the future. This may lead to tests being offered to other family members to find out if they have the same condition.

question: How are personal information and public interests protected when using stored blood spot cards?
answer: Personal information and public interests are protected when using stored blood spot cards by strict regulations and laws that dictate who can access these cards and how they can be used. Ethical approval is required for any research involving these cards. Parental consent is required before a baby's blood spot card can be used for any purpose, and anonymity and confidentiality steps are taken to keep personal information private.

question: What is primary haemochromatosis?
answer: Primary haemochromatosis is an inherited condition caused by genetic mutations. In some countries, blood spot cards have been used to find out how many people carry these mutations.

question: How long should the blood spot cards be stored?
answer: Under the code of practice, it is recommended that blood spot cards are stored for at least five years. Laboratory directors store them and ensure that the guidelines are followed.

question: What are the laws that cover the use of newborn blood spot cards?
answer: The laws that cover the use of newborn blood spot cards include the Data Protection Act 1998, the Health and Social Care Act 2001 and the Human Tissue Act 2004. Guidance has been developed with careful reference to these laws to ensure that the cards are used in accordance with them.

question: Is parental consent required before using the newborn blood spot card for any purpose?
answer: Yes, parental consent is required before a newborn blood spot card can be used for any purpose. Before parents are offered newborn blood spot screening for their baby, they are given a pre-screening leaflet and have a discussion with their midwife. This is to help them make an informed choice.

question: What is newborn screening?
answer: Newborn screening is a set of tests that are offered to all newborn babies to check if they have any serious health conditions that are not apparent when babies are born. These tests are done to help identify and treat any potential health problems early on, before they become more serious.

question: Why is newborn screening offered?
answer: Newborn screening is offered to identify any health problems in babies that need immediate medical attention. Early detection and treatment of these conditions can prevent severe disability, long-term illness or even death.

question: What are some of the conditions that the newborn blood spot test checks for?
answer: The newborn blood spot test checks for nine rare but serious health conditions that include phenylketonuria, cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease, and maple syrup urine disease, among others.

question: Is newborn screening necessary?
answer: While most babies are healthy and will not have any of the conditions that the newborn screening tests are looking for, early detection of health problems can make a significant difference in preventing severe disabilities or even death. Therefore, newborn screening is necessary for all newborns.

question: Are newborn screening tests harmful to babies?
answer: No, newborn screening tests are quick, safe, and not harmful to babies. They are typically done through a heel prick to collect a small blood sample or through a hearing test, which involves placing a small probe in the baby's ear.

question: What is the newborn hearing test?
answer: The newborn hearing test is a screening test that checks your newborn baby's hearing within the first few weeks of life. It is done to identify any hearing loss early on so that early intervention and treatment can be started to prevent long-term problems with speech and language development.

question: Is the newborn physical examination necessary?
answer: Yes, the newborn physical examination is necessary. It is a thorough examination that is offered to every baby soon after birth to check their eyes, heart, hips, and in boys, testicles, to identify potential health problems that may need further testing or treatment.

question: When is the newborn physical examination carried out?
answer: The newborn physical examination is carried out within 72 hours of birth and again at 6 to 8 weeks of age. This is because some conditions can take a while to develop, and the follow-up examination helps to identify any new problems that may have arisen.

question: Can parents decline newborn screening tests?
answer: Yes, parents can decline newborn screening tests if they wish. However, it is recommended that newborn screening is done to identify and treat any potential health problems early on, and parents should discuss any concerns they have with their healthcare provider.

question: What should parents expect during the newborn blood spot test?
answer: During the newborn blood spot test, a healthcare professional will prick your baby's heel and collect a few drops of blood on a special card. Although the heel prick may be uncomfortable and your baby may cry, the procedure is over very quickly. The blood sample will then be sent off for testing to check for rare but serious health conditions.

question: What should I do if one of my babies seems to be feeding more or less than the other?
answer: If one baby seems to be feeding more or less than the other, or you have any other concerns about your babies, talk to your health visitor.

question: Is it possible to breastfeed twins, triplets or more?
answer: It's perfectly possible to breastfeed twins, triplets or more. Lots of twins are breastfed until they start eating solid foods.

question: What are the benefits of breast milk for multiple babies?
answer: The benefits of breast milk for your babies are the same as for single babies. However, as multiple babies are more likely to be born prematurely, there are extra benefits to breast milk, such as containing proteins and antibodies to protect your babies against infections.

question: What should I do if my babies are very tiny or sick when they're born?
answer: If your babies are very tiny or sick when they're born, you may need to express your breast milk to begin with. Your expressed milk may be fed to your babies through a thin tube that passes through the nose and into the stomach.

question: Is formula feeding more expensive than breastfeeding when you have twins or more?
answer: Formula feeding is more expensive than breastfeeding when you have twins or more.

question: Should I feed all of my babies together or separately when formula feeding?
answer: As with breastfeeding, you'll need to decide whether you're going to feed your babies together or separately when formula feeding.

question: What should I do if I need to go back to work while formula feeding my multiples?
answer: If you need to go back to work while formula feeding your multiples, you may want to consider investing in a good breast pump so that you can continue to provide breast milk for your babies.

question: When can I start giving my twins solid foods?
answer: When your babies are around 6 months old, you can give them their first solid foods.

question: What positions should I try when breastfeeding twins?
answer: You may like to try a few breastfeeding positions to see which suits you best.

question: Where can I find more information on feeding twins or more?
answer: You can visit the Twins Trust charity's or Multiple Births Foundation websites for more information on breastfeeding and formula feeding twins or more.

question: What should I do if I need help feeding and caring for my newborn twins at the hospital?
answer: Hospital staff will assist you in feeding and caring for your newborn twins at the hospital. If you need help, don't hesitate to ask for it.

question: Is it possible to have a private room to bond with my newborn twins at the hospital?
answer: Yes, some hospitals allow parents to have a private room where they can get to know their babies in peace. You may want to ask if this is an option for you.

question: What should I do if my newborn twins need special care after birth?
answer: If your newborn twins need special neonatal care, hospital staff will show you how to touch and care for them even if they need to be nursed in an incubator. You'll be encouraged to breastfeed them as breast milk is best for premature babies.

question: What should I consider if I'm likely to give birth early to my twins?
answer: If you think you might give birth early to your twins, you should check if the hospital has a transitional care unit, cots that allow co-bedding, and support from a community neonatal nurse. You may also need to move to another hospital where there are enough beds for both your babies.

question: What should I do if one of my twins can feed effectively and the other can't while breastfeeding?
answer: If one of your twins can't feed effectively while breastfeeding, you may need to put the twin who can feed on the breast to encourage milk to flow for both babies. Talk to your healthcare provider for more information on feeding twins and multiples.

question: How can I cope with caring for my newborn twins at home?
answer: To cope with caring for your newborn twins at home, you can create a routine that works for the whole family, keep nappy changing gear on different floors, make double portions of food and freeze it, and ask for help from family and friends. You can also limit visitors and schedule follow-up appointments later in the day.

question: How often should I bathe my newborn twins at home?
answer: You don't need to bathe your newborn twins every day. Two or three times a week are enough. You may consider bathing them on alternate nights so you can get to know them individually.

question: Is it normal to feel overwhelmed when dividing attention between two or more babies?
answer: Feeling overwhelmed when dividing your attention between multiple babies is a normal feeling. You can seek help and support from your health visitor, GP, family or friends.

question: Can I visit my twin baby in hospital with their sibling?
answer: You should ask if you can bring the sibling of your twin baby to the hospital and if co-bedding is allowed during visits. Visiting your twin baby in the hospital can help with bonding and caring for both babies.

question: What should I do if I want my babies to sleep together in one cot?
answer: You should check if your hospital has cots that allow co-bedding if you want your babies to sleep in one cot. It's advisable to consult with hospital staff to ensure the safety of the babies.

question: How can I find support as a single parent?
answer: As a single parent, you can accept help from relatives and friends willing to lend a hand for time out, babysitting, and school runs. You can also suggest a "swap" arrangement with another parent, so you take it in turns to look after each other's children. Moreover, it is possible to suggest a regular evening's babysitting by a trusted relative or friend. If you do not know people locally, ask your health visitor what local groups are available in your area or contact Gingerbread, a charity for single parent families that can put you in touch with other parents in a similar situation and give you much-needed support.

question: What can I do if I want to co-parent but live apart from my child's other parent?
answer: As a lone parent, it's important to hide your negative feelings from your child and let them build their own relationship with their other parent. It's usually better for children to see both parents regularly, even if you start new relationships. Of course, this does not apply if your ex-partner is violent or abusive towards you or your child. Moreover, if at first, you find your child behaves badly when they come home after a visit, the best way to deal with this is to be reassuring and calm. In the end, your child will learn to look forward to visits and coming home. Also, you'll almost certainly need to talk about your own feelings. Try to find another adult to talk to. Gingerbread has more advice on making arrangements for your children.

question: How can Gingerbread help single parents?
answer: Gingerbread is a charity for single parent families that can put you in touch with other parents in a similar situation and give you much-needed support. They offer free information packs for lone parents and can give you independent advice about benefits, housing, and child maintenance problems.

question: What does the Child Maintenance Service do?
answer: The Child Maintenance Service can arrange child maintenance on your behalf if you cannot reach an agreement with the other parent about child maintenance arrangements. They can collect maintenance payments from the paying parent and pass them on to the receiving parent. They can also help you find the other parent if you do not know where they live, and help sort out any disagreements about parentage. If you want to use the Child Maintenance Service, you'll need to contact them first. You can call them on 0800 988 0988.

question: How can a lone parent get financial help for a disabled child?
answer: Lone parent carers of disabled children can get support, and financial help is available if they need any aids or adaptations around the home. They may also be eligible for a range of benefits and tax credits, including the Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children, Universal Credit, and tax credits. If their child is 16 or over, they may be able to claim the Personal Independence Payment (PIP). You can find more information on benefits and tax credits on the Contact website or call the Gingerbread helpline for free on 0808 802 0925. Some charities and organizations issue grants to parents who have a child with a disability or long-term illness. Call Contact's free helpline on 0808 808 3555 for a list of these organizations.

question: What should I do if I don't have friends or family around to help me as a single parent?
answer: If you don't have friends or family around to help you as a single parent, ask your health visitor what local groups are available in your area or contact Gingerbread, a charity for single parent families that can put you in touch with other parents in a similar situation and give you much-needed support.

question: Can I get advice about child maintenance from Gingerbread?
answer: Yes. Gingerbread is a charity for single parent families that can give you independent advice about benefits, housing, and child maintenance problems.

question: What benefits can a lone parent claim for a disabled child?
answer: Lone parents of disabled children may be eligible for benefits and tax credits, including the Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children and Universal Credit. If their child is 16 or over, they may be able to claim the Personal Independence Payment (PIP).

question: How can I talk to my child about co-parenting if I'm a single parent?
answer: As a lone parent, it's important to hide your negative feelings from your child and let them build their own relationship with their other parent. Try to be reassuring and calm when your child comes back from a visit, especially if they are upset or confused. Also, use clear and straightforward language when you talk about co-parenting with them. Let them know that they are loved and that their parents will always be there for them, even if they do not live together anymore.

question: What can I do if I need a break from parenting as a single parent?
answer: If you need a break from parenting as a single parent, do not be afraid to ask for help from friends and family. You may also find that other single parents are a good source of support. Alternatively, you could suggest a "swap" arrangement with another parent, so you take it in turns to look after each other's children or suggest a regular evening's babysitting by a trusted relative or friend.

question: What are the symptoms of "baby blues"?
answer: Symptoms of "baby blues" include feeling emotional and bursting into tears for no apparent reason, feeling irritable or touchy, low mood, and anxiety and restlessness.

question: How long does "baby blues" last?
answer: "Baby blues" usually only last for a few days.

question: What is postnatal depression?
answer: Postnatal depression is a type of depression that affects around 1 in 10 women after giving birth. It can start at any point in the first year after giving birth and may develop suddenly or gradually.

question: What are the common emotional signs of postnatal depression?
answer: The common emotional signs of postnatal depression include loss of interest in the world around you, feelings of hopelessness, not being able to stop crying, feelings of not being able to cope, not being able to enjoy anything, memory loss or being unable to concentrate, and excessive anxiety about your baby.

question: What are the other signs of postnatal depression?
answer: Other signs of postnatal depression may include sleeplessness, extreme tiredness, feeling generally unwell, anxiety, and loss of appetite.

question: How can postnatal depression be treated?
answer: There are three main types of treatments for postnatal depression: self-help, psychological therapy, and antidepressants. You can talk to a GP about the pros and cons of different treatments so you can decide together what's best for you.

question: What should I do if I think I have postnatal depression?
answer: If you think you may be depressed, talk to a GP, midwife or health visitor as soon as possible so you can access the support you need.

question: What should I avoid if I think I have postnatal depression?
answer: You should avoid alcohol if you think you have postnatal depression. It can affect your mood, judgement, self-control, and co-ordination, and it may make your symptoms worse.

question: What is postpartum psychosis?
answer: Postpartum psychosis, also called puerperal psychosis, is a rare severe psychiatric illness that requires medical or hospital treatment after the birth of a baby. It can develop within hours of childbirth and is very serious, needing urgent attention. Only 1 or 2 mothers in 1,000 develop this illness.

question: What is postnatal post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)?
answer: Postnatal post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is often the result of a traumatic birth or other types of trauma. The symptoms of postnatal PTSD can occur alone or in addition to the symptoms of postnatal depression. The symptoms can develop straight after the birth or months afterwards.

question: How can I deal with the grief after the death of my child?
answer: You need to let yourself grieve in your own way. If you need to cry, do. It may be the only way you can let your feelings out. If you feel angry or blame yourself or others, it's important to talk about it. You may also feel anger, bewilderment and even guilt. All these feelings are important and shouldn't be set aside quickly or hidden away.

question: How do I explain the death of my child to my other children?
answer: If you have other children, explain to them what's happened as simply and honestly as you can. Sometimes older children worry the death is linked to something they've done. They may be very quiet or behave very badly for a while. It's not always easy to give them the love and reassurance they need when you're grieving yourself. It can help to get support from others close to your child.

question: What should I do if I need help or advice after the death of my partner or child?
answer: If you need help or advice, contact your GP. They can give you details of support groups in your area. Talking to someone outside the family, such as a close friend, your doctor, health visitor, hospital staff or a religious leader, can be helpful.

question: What are some common feelings experienced when a child dies?
answer: You may feel angry, bewilderment and even guilt. All these feelings are important and shouldn't be set aside quickly or hidden away. The death of a child is a loss like no other. When a child dies before their parents, it feels so wrong that great shock is added to the enormous grief and sadness you'll already be feeling.

question: What are the organisations that offer support and advice for parents who lost a child?
answer: These organisations can offer support and advice, and put you in touch with other parents who've had a similar experience: Sands, The Lullaby Trust, The Compassionate Friends, Cruse Bereavement Care, Winston's Wish, Child Bereavement UK, and The Child Death Helpline.

question: What should I do if I feel numb after losing my partner?
answer: Don't be afraid to rely on family and friends for help and support, for yourself and your baby. You may need urgent financial advice and support. If you feel numb and think you'll never get over what's happened, that may be true, but you'll eventually learn to live with it.

question: How can I remember my partner after their death?
answer: It may help you to think of ways to remember your partner. Consider the service or ceremony you may want to have and any mementos you may want to keep. Do what feels right for you.

question: What can I do if I am having trouble coping with my grief after the death of my partner or child?
answer: Contact your GP if you need help or advice. They can give you details of support groups in your area. It can be difficult at first to cope with the outside world and other people. You may find even people who are close to you don't know what to say or avoid you. Take the support that's offered and do what feels right for you.

question: When should I register my baby with a GP?
answer: You should register your baby with your GP as early as possible in case you need their help.

question: What services do health visitors provide?
answer: Health visitors offer help to you, your family and your new baby to stay healthy. They provide advice and suggest where to find help, put you in touch with groups where you can meet other parents, and offer regular baby health and development reviews and vaccinations.

question: What are Child health clinics?
answer: Child health clinics are run by health visitors and GPs. They offer regular baby health and development reviews and vaccinations. You can also talk about any problems to do with your child, but if your child is ill and likely to need treatment, see your GP. Some child health clinics also run parent and baby, breastfeeding, and peer support groups.

question: What are Sure Start children's centres?
answer: Sure Start children's centres provide family health and support services, early learning and full-day or temporary care for children from birth to 5 years. They also provide advice and information for parents on a range of issues, from parenting to training and employment opportunities.

question: What is FIS?
answer: Family Information Service (FIS) aims to help you support your children by providing information for parents. They offer information about local childcare services and availability and can help if you need childcare for a child with a disability or special needs.

question: What are advice centres?
answer: Advice centres are non-profit agencies that give advice on issues such as benefits and housing.

question: What services can I find on the contact.org.uk website?
answer: The contact.org.uk website provides support, advice and information for parents with disabled children.

question: What is Gingerbread?
answer: Gingerbread is an organization that provides help and advice on the issues that matter to lone parents.

question: How can I find out about local parent and baby groups?
answer: You can find out about local parent and baby groups by asking your health visitor or GP, looking on noticeboards and for leaflets at your local child health clinic or health centre, searching on the internet or on social media, or checking your local council's website.

question: What should I do if I need language support?
answer: If you need language support, ask your health visitor what's available in your area. There may be support available if English is not your first language.

question: When can I start having sex after giving birth?
answer: There are no specific rules on when to start having sex again after giving birth. However, you may want to wait until your body has fully healed and recovered. Talk with your partner and consider using a personal lubricant to make the experience more comfortable.

question: What should I do if sex hurts after giving birth?
answer: If sex hurts after giving birth, it's important to communicate with your partner and say so. You can still be intimate without penetration, such as through mutual masturbation. Using a personal lubricant may also be helpful, as hormonal changes after childbirth can make your vagina feel drier than usual.

question: Can I get pregnant again even if I'm breastfeeding and my periods haven't started?
answer: Yes, it is possible to get pregnant as little as 3 weeks after giving birth, even if you are breastfeeding and your periods haven't started. It's important to use contraception every time you have sex if you don't want to get pregnant again.

question: When should I start using another form of contraception if I'm using breastfeeding as a natural form of contraception?
answer: It's important to start using another form of contraception if your baby is more than 6 months old, you give them anything other than breast milk (such as a dummy, formula or solid foods), your periods start again (even light spotting counts), you stop night feeding, you start to breastfeed less often, or there are longer intervals between feeds, both during the day and at night.

question: What hormonal changes can happen after giving birth?
answer: Hormonal changes after giving birth can make your vagina feel drier than usual, which can make sex uncomfortable. These changes can also affect your menstrual cycle and breast milk production. Talk with your GP or midwife if you have any concerns or questions.

question: What should I do if I'm worried about changes to my body or getting pregnant again?
answer: If you're worried about changes to your body after giving birth or getting pregnant again, talk with your partner and healthcare provider. You can discuss contraception options and ways to address any physical or emotional concerns. Remember, it's important to prioritize your health and well-being.

question: Can men worry about hurting their partner during sex after giving birth?
answer: It is possible for men to worry about hurting their partner during sex after giving birth. It's important to communicate openly and honestly with your partner and to take things slowly. Engaging in non-penetrative intimacy, such as mutual masturbation, can be a good way to establish intimacy and share pleasure.

question: Do I need to use contraception the first time I have sex after giving birth?
answer: Yes, it's important to use contraception every time you have sex after giving birth, including the first time. You can discuss contraception options with your healthcare provider and choose the best method for you based on your health history and lifestyle.

question: How long should I wait before having sex after giving birth?
answer: There are no specific rules on how long you should wait before having sex after giving birth. It's important to listen to your body and communicate with your partner. You may want to wait until your body has healed and recovered, and consider using a personal lubricant to make the experience more comfortable.

question: Where can I go for help with contraception after giving birth?
answer: You can discuss contraception options and receive support from your GP, health visitor, family planning clinic, or NHS contraception service. You can also use interactive tools provided by sexual health charities Brook and FPA to help you decide which method of contraception is best for you.

question: How often should I bathe my newborn baby?
answer: You do not need to bathe your baby in the first few days. You may prefer to wash their face, neck, hands and bottom carefully instead. This is sometimes called topping and tailing. Choose a time when your baby is awake and content. Make sure the room is warm and get everything ready beforehand.

question: How can I reduce the risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS)?
answer: Putting your baby on their back to sleep, in a cot in the same room as you, for the first 6 months is one way to reduce your baby's risk even further. Not smoking during pregnancy or breastfeeding, and not letting anyone else smoke in the same room as your baby, will also help protect them.

question: Why is my baby constantly crying?
answer: Crying is your baby's way of telling you they need comfort and care. But it's not always easy to work out what they want. Find out why your baby may be crying and how to soothe them.

question: When should we bathe our newborn baby?
answer: You do not need to bathe your baby in the first few days. It is best to wait until their umbilical cord stump falls off and their circumcision has healed. Your baby's neck and face can be gently washed with a damp cloth between baths if needed.

question: What can we do if our baby has nappy rash?
answer: If your baby has nappy rash, you should change their nappy frequently and let them go nappy-free as often as possible, clean the area gently with cotton wool and warm water or fragrance-free baby wipes, and apply a thin layer of barrier cream to protect the skin until the rash clears up.

question: How can I tell if my baby is getting enough milk during breastfeeding?
answer: You can tell if your baby is getting enough milk by checking the number of wet and soiled nappies. After the first few days, your baby should have at least six wet nappies a day, and their urine should be pale and not too smelly. Your baby should also have at least two or three bowel movements that are yellow and loose or soft. If you're unsure, get in touch with a professional.

question: When can I expect my baby to start sleeping for longer periods of time at night?
answer: As your baby grows, they'll gradually start to need fewer night feeds and will sleep for longer at night. It's normal for new babies to only sleep for 2 to 3 hours at a time through the night, as well as during the day.

question: How often should I change my baby's nappy?
answer: Babies need frequent nappy changes. Do not leave them in a wet or dirty nappy for too long because their wee and the bacteria in their poo may make their skin sore and lead to nappy rash.

question: What should we do with the umbilical cord stump of our baby?
answer: The baby's umbilical cord stump should be kept clean and dry. Sponge baths are recommended for the first two weeks after cord separation. You can clean the area around the stump with a sponge or cloth dipped in warm water and antibacterial soap or plain water only.

question: Is it safe to leave my baby in a room alone?
answer: No, you should never leave your baby in a room alone as they are completely dependent on you for their safety and well-being. Always keep your baby within your line of sight and within earshot.

question: What physical problems can occur after pregnancy?
answer: Various physical problems can occur after pregnancy, including incontinence or a heavy feeling between your vagina and anus, back pain, and separated stomach muscles. These problems can be related to pregnancy or birth, or the things you do while caring for young children.

question: What can I do to help with incontinence or a heavy feeling between my vagina and anus?
answer: You may need to strengthen the muscles around your bladder by doing pelvic floor exercises to improve these conditions. You can do these exercises lying down, sitting or standing. With practice, they can be done anywhere and at any time.

question: When is a good time to talk to your GP about any physical or mental health problems you've had since giving birth?
answer: Your postnatal check at around 6 to 8 weeks after the birth of your baby is a good time to talk to the GP about any physical or mental health problems you’ve had since the birth.

question: What is diastasis recti or divarication?
answer: Diastasis recti is when the two muscles that run down the middle of your stomach separate during pregnancy. It’s common, and happens because your growing womb pushes the muscles apart, making them longer and weaker. It is also called divarication.

question: How can pelvic floor muscle exercises help after pregnancy?
answer: Pelvic floor exercises help strengthen the muscles around your bladder, vagina and bottom, which can help to stop incontinence, improve prolapse, and make sex better too.

question: How can I do stomach exercises to tone my stomach muscles after pregnancy?
answer: Lie on your side with your knees slightly bent for a stomach exercise. Let your stomach relax and breathe in gently. As you breathe out, gently draw in the lower part of your stomach like a corset, narrowing your waistline. Squeeze your pelvic floor muscles at the same time. Hold for a count of 10, breathing normally, then gently release. Repeat up to 10 times.

question: What are some practical tips to relieve back pain after having a baby?
answer: Some practical tips to relieve back pain after having a baby include sitting with your back well-supported and straight while feeding your baby, kneeling or squatting (not bending your back) to do tasks that are near the floor, changing a nappy on a raised surface, and keeping your back straight when lifting or pushing a pram.

question: How often should I do pelvic floor exercises after pregnancy?
answer: Aim to build up to 10 repetitions of each pelvic floor exercise, at least 3 times a day. It's important to keep breathing normally while you do these exercises. Make sure you do not pull in your stomach when you squeeze. Sitting on the toilet can be a good reminder to do your exercises. Just make sure you do them after you've finished.

question: When is it recommended to start introducing solid foods to a baby?
answer: Introducing solid foods to a baby should start around 6 months of age.

question: What is the reason for waiting until around 6 months to introduce solids to a baby?
answer: It is a good idea to wait until around 6 months to introduce solids to a baby because infants get the energy and nutrients they need from breast milk or formula until around that time, and waiting gives the baby time to develop the necessary skills to cope with solid foods.

question: What are the clear signs that show a baby is ready for solid foods?
answer: The 3 clear signs are that the baby can sit upright and hold their head steady, co-ordinate their eyes, hands and mouth so they can look at the food, pick it up and put it in their mouth by themselves, and swallow food rather than spit it back out.

question: What is the importance of getting a baby used to new tastes and textures?
answer: Getting a baby used to new tastes and textures is important as it can help set the child up for a lifetime of healthier eating.

question: What are some tips for getting a baby off to a good start with solid foods?
answer: Some tips include being patient, allowing plenty of time, going at the baby's pace, and giving lots of encouragement and praise.

question: What are the benefits of breastfeeding for a baby's first 6 months of life?
answer: Breast milk is the best food for a baby during its first 6 months of life because it is free, always available and at the perfect temperature, and is tailor-made for the baby.

question: What should be done before giving solid foods to a baby?
answer: Before giving solid foods to a baby, it's important to take extra care with food safety and hygiene, such as washing hands, washing and peeling fruit and vegetables, and avoiding hard foods like whole nuts or raw carrot or apple.

question: What are some examples of finger foods that can be given to a baby?
answer: Some examples include soft cooked vegetables, fruits, grabbable bits of avocado, cooked starchy foods, pulses, fish without bones, hardboiled eggs, and meat without bones.

question: What is baby-led weaning?
answer: Baby-led weaning means giving a baby only finger foods and letting the baby feed itself from the start.

question: How much milk per day do formula-fed babies need when starting solid foods?
answer: As a guide, formula-fed babies may need around 600ml of milk a day when starting solid foods.

question: What should be included in my baby's diet?
answer: Your baby's diet should consist of a variety of food groups including fruit and vegetables, starchy foods, sources of protein, and dairy products. It is also important to include iron-rich foods such as meat, fish, fortified breakfast cereals, dark green vegetables, beans, and lentils in their meals.

question: When should I offer finger foods to my baby?
answer: As your baby becomes a more confident eater, you can offer more mashed, lumpy, and finger foods. Providing finger foods as part of each meal helps encourage infants to feed themselves, develop hand and eye coordination, and learn to bite off, chew, and swallow pieces of soft food.

question: How many meals and milk feeds should my 10-month-old baby have in a day?
answer: From about 10 months, your baby should now be having three meals a day (breakfast, lunch, and tea), in addition to their usual milk feeds. Around this age, your baby may have about three milk feeds a day (for instance, after breakfast, after lunch, and before bed).

question: What should be avoided while feeding babies and young children?
answer: Babies and young children should not be given foods that are high in salt or sugar, or drinks that are not suitable for their age. Rice drinks should also be avoided for children under five years old due to their high levels of arsenic.

question: When can I start giving my child whole cows' milk?
answer: Once your child is 12 months old, they can drink whole cows' milk. Choose full-fat dairy products, as children under 2 years old need the vitamins and extra energy found in them.

question: What should I include in my child's meals from the age of 12 months?
answer: From 12 months, your child should be eating three meals a day that include a variety of different foods. This should include a minimum of four servings a day of starchy food, four servings of fruit and vegetables, and one serving a day of protein from animal sources such as meat, fish, and eggs or two servings of vegetable sources such as dhal, beans, chickpeas, and lentils.

question: What are some healthy snack options for my child?
answer: Healthy snack options for your child include fresh fruits such as apple, banana, or small pieces of soft, ripe, peeled pear or peach, cooked or raw vegetables like broccoli florets, carrot sticks or cucumber sticks, pasteurized plain full-fat yoghurt, cheese sticks (choose a lower salt option), toast, pitta or chapatti fingers, and unsalted and unsweetened rice or corn cakes.

question: When can I start giving my child unsweetened milk alternatives?
answer: You can give your child unsweetened calcium-fortified milk alternatives, such as soya, oat, or almond drinks, from the age of 1 as a part of a healthy, balanced diet.

question: What should be included in my child's diet to ensure they get enough iron?
answer: It is important to include iron-rich foods such as meat, fish, fortified breakfast cereals, dark green vegetables, beans, and lentils in your child's diet. These iron-rich foods should be included in each meal to ensure your child is getting the necessary energy and nutrients they need.

question: Till when can I breastfeed my baby and how much milk should they be drinking?
answer: The World Health Organization recommends that all babies are breastfed for up to 2 years or longer. Your baby may have about 3 milk feeds a day till about 10 months old. Breastfed babies will adapt their milk consumption as their food intake changes. As a guide, babies fed infant formula will drink about 400ml daily.

question: How can I keep my child safe from food bugs?
answer: Babies and young children are especially vulnerable to bacteria that can cause food poisoning. To keep your child safe, you should always wash your hands before preparing food and after touching raw meat, chicken, fish, shellfish, and eggs. You should also make sure that your child's hands are clean before feeding, teach them to wash their hands after touching pets and going to the toilet, and before eating. Keep surfaces clean and any pets away from food or surfaces where food is prepared or eaten. Thoroughly wash all bowls and spoons used for feeding in hot soapy water, and make sure chopping boards and utensils are also kept clean. You should also cook all food thoroughly and cool it until lukewarm before giving it to your child.

question: How should I store food for my child?
answer: You should cool food as quickly as possible (ideally within 1 to 2 hours) and put it in the fridge or freezer. Food placed in the fridge should be eaten within 2 days. Rice should be cooled as quickly as possible (within 1 hour) and put in the fridge or freezer. Rice placed in the fridge should be eaten within 24 hours and never reheated more than once. Frozen food should be thoroughly defrosted before reheating. The safest way to do this is to leave it in the fridge overnight or use the defrost setting on a microwave. When you're reheating food, make sure it's steaming hot all the way through, then let it cool down before giving it to your child. If you're using a microwave, always stir the food and check the temperature before feeding it to your child. Don't reheat cooked food more than once.

question: How can I avoid food poisoning from raw meats?
answer: You should always keep raw meats and eggs covered and away from other foods in the fridge. Cook all food thoroughly and cool it until lukewarm before giving it to your child. Store raw meats in clean, covered containers at the bottom of the fridge to prevent any drips from falling onto other foods. Use separate utensils, cutting boards, and dishes for raw and cooked foods. You should also wash your hands before preparing food and after touching raw meat, chicken, fish, shellfish, and eggs.

question: Should I wash and peel fruits and vegetables before giving them to my child?
answer: Yes, you should wash and peel fruits and vegetables such as apples and carrots before giving them to your child. This will help to remove any dirt or bacteria that may be on the surface of the fruit or vegetable. It's important to ensure that your child is getting all the nutrients they need, so it's best to choose a variety of different fruits and vegetables to offer them.

question: Can I give my child raw eggs?
answer: Hens' eggs stamped with the British Lion mark, or produced under the "Laid in Britain" scheme, are fine for babies and children to have raw (for example, in homemade mayonnaise) or lightly cooked.
