However, it's important to avoid eating raw or lightly cooked shellfish. Babies and children should only eat shellfish that's been thoroughly cooked.

question: How should I clean bottles and utensils used for feeding?
answer: Thoroughly wash all bowls and spoons used for feeding in hot soapy water, and make sure chopping boards and utensils are also kept clean. You should also sterilize bottles and teats until your child is at least 12 months old. After this, washing bottles in hot, soapy water should be sufficient.

question: How can I cool food quickly?
answer: To cool food quickly, put it in an airtight container and hold it under a cold running tap. Stir it from time to time so it cools consistently all the way through. You should ideally cool the food within 1 to 2 hours of cooking and put it in the fridge or freezer. Food placed in the fridge should be eaten within 2 days.

question: Can I give my child half-eaten foods?
answer: No, it's not safe to save and reuse foods that your child has half eaten. Bacteria from their mouth can contaminate the food, increasing the risk of food poisoning. Instead, throw any uneaten food away and offer your child fresh food at the next mealtime.

question: What should I do if my child is choking?
answer: Always stay with your child while they're eating in case they choke. Find out how to stop a child from choking. If your child is choking, stay calm and encourage them to cough and try to clear the obstruction themselves. If this doesn't work, lean them forward and give them up to five sharp blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. If this doesn't work, call an ambulance.

question: Can I feed my child on the potty?
answer: No, don't give children food or drink when they're sitting on the potty. This can be a choking hazard, and it's important to avoid any distractions while your child is eating. Instead, make sure that your child is sitting in a safe and comfortable position while they eat, and supervise them at all times.

question: What should I do if my child refuses to eat new foods?
answer: Gradually introduce other foods and keep going back to the foods your child did not like before. Children's tastes change. One day they'll hate something, but a month later they may love it. Keep offering a variety of foods – it may take lots of attempts before your child accepts some foods.

question: Is it normal for toddlers to refuse to eat new foods?
answer: Yes, it's perfectly normal for toddlers to refuse to eat or even taste new foods.

question: What should I do if my child only eats a small portion of their meal?
answer: Give small portions and praise your child for eating, even if they only eat a little.

question: How should I encourage my child to eat new foods?
answer: Give your child the same food as the rest of the family, but remember n ot to add salt to your child's food. Check the label of any food product you use to make family meals. Try to eat with them as often as you can.

question: How should I handle my frustration if my child refuses to eat a particular food?
answer: If your child rejects the food, do not force them to eat it. Just take the food away without saying anything. Try to stay calm, even if it's very frustrating. Try the food again another time.

question: Can I use food as a reward for my child?
answer: No, do not use food as a reward. Your child may start to think of sweets as nice and vegetables as nasty. Instead, reward them with a trip to the park or promise to play a game with them.

question: How many healthy snacks should I give my child between meals?
answer: Do not give your child too many snacks between meals – 2 healthy snacks a day is plenty.

question: Should I make mealtimes enjoyable for my child?
answer: Yes, make mealtimes enjoyable and not just about eating. Sit down and chat about other things.

question: What are the 4 main food groups for babies?
answer: The 4 main food groups for babies are fruit and vegetables, starchy carbohydrates, dairy, and pulses, meat, and other proteins. It's important to give them a wide variety of foods from these groups to set them up for a lifetime of healthy eating.

question: How can I get my baby used to eating a variety of foods?
answer: You can get your baby used to eating a variety of foods by offering different foods and gradually introducing new ones. Keep offering a variety of foods, including less sweet vegetables like broccoli, cauliflower, and spinach. Encourage your baby to feed themselves with their fingers and allow plenty of time for eating at first.

question: How should I offer my baby new foods?
answer: You should offer your baby new foods gradually and with patience. It may take 10 or more attempts for your baby to accept new foods, particularly as they get older. Encourage your baby to feed themselves with their fingers and offer less sweet vegetables from the start.

question: Can I give my baby snacks?
answer: Babies under 9 months old do not need snacks. If you think your baby is hungry in between meals, offer extra milk feeds instead. Avoid giving your baby sugary drinks and snacks high in sugar, fat, or salt, as these can fill them up so they're not hungry for healthier food.

question: What finger foods should I give my baby?
answer: As a guide, the best finger foods for babies are soft or cooked foods that can be cut up into pieces big enough for your baby to hold in their fist and stick out of the top of it. Pieces about the size of your own finger work well.

question: Should I worry if my baby doesn't eat a lot?
answer: There will be days when your baby eats more, some days when they eat less, and some days when they reject everything. This is perfectly normal. Do not focus on what your baby eats in a meal or a day. It's more helpful to think about what they eat over a week.

question: How can I make sure my baby is sitting safely during mealtimes?
answer: Make sure your baby is sitting safely in an upright position so they can swallow properly. Keep distractions like the television, phone, or tablet to a minimum during mealtimes.

question: Are packaged baby snacks healthy for my baby?
answer: Packaged baby snacks, such as rusks, baby biscuits, and baby biscotti should not form part of your baby's diet, as they may contain lots of sugar. It's best to avoid getting your baby used to these snacks as it may make them more likely to want them as they get older.

question: Can I give my baby homemade food?
answer: Yes, you can make healthier homemade food from simple ingredients with no added sugar or salt, which can also be cheaper than shop-bought baby foods. This also helps your baby get used to family foods.

question: What if my baby doesn't like a new food I give them?
answer: It's normal for babies to make funny faces when trying new foods, but this does not mean they don't like it. They're just getting used to new flavors and textures. It may take 10 or even more attempts for your baby to accept new foods, particularly as they get older. Always go at your baby's pace and stop when they show you they have had enough.

question: What are some healthy snack options for young children?
answer: Healthy snack options for young children include raw vegetable sticks with hummus, a piece of fruit, plain yogurt with sliced banana, a slice of toast with cheese spread or peanut butter, crackers, breadsticks, or unsalted rice cakes with cheese and vegetable sticks, and a bowl of unsweetened cereal with whole milk.

question: What are some good sandwich fillings to pack in my child's lunchbox?
answer: Good sandwich fillings for a child's lunchbox include canned tuna or salmon, hummus, hard or cream cheese, egg, or peanut butter. It is important to check for food allergies before including items such as egg or peanut butter.

question: What are some healthier sweet options to pack in my child's lunchbox?
answer: Healthier sweet options to pack in a child's lunchbox include yogurt, fromage frais, a scone, or a currant bun.

question: Can high-fiber foods be harmful to young children?
answer: While high-fiber foods are important for a healthy diet, foods such as wholemeal bread and pasta, brown rice, and wholegrain breakfast cereals can fill up small tummies and leave little room for other necessary nutrients. As a result, it is recommended to avoid giving only wholegrain or high-fiber foods to children under five years old.

question: What should I do if my child only drinks sugary drinks?
answer: Drinking sugary drinks can lead to tooth decay, and it can be difficult to break the habit. One approach is to dilute the sugary drinks with water gradually over time, so the change is not very noticeable to the child. Water and whole milk are the best drinks for young children.

question: What can I pack in my child's lunchbox when they go to nursery?
answer: In addition to good sandwich fillings, a child's lunchbox could also include vegetable sticks such as carrots or cucumber, bite-sized fruit like a peeled satsuma or washed seedless grapes, and a box of raisins eaten alongside their lunch. Parents should consult with the child's nursery for any food policies

question: Are there any benefits available to help me buy healthy food for my child?
answer: The Healthy Start scheme may be able to help with the purchase of food and milk for the child if the parent has children under four years old and receives certain benefits like income support. Additionally, if the parent is at least ten weeks pregnant and receives certain benefits or if the parent is under 18 and is pregnant, they may be eligible for the Healthy Start scheme. The scheme provides a Healthy Start card that can be used to buy certain types of milk, infant formula, fruits, and vegetables.

question: What should I do if my child has a food allergy?
answer: If the child has a food allergy, be sure to notify their nursery or childminder. Parents should also be cautious about the foods and fillings that they pack in the child's lunchbox.

question: What drinks are recommended for toddlers?
answer: Water and whole milk are the best drinks for toddlers. Parents should consult their pediatrician for additional recommendations.

question: How can I keep my child's food safe and cool when they go to nursery?
answer: If lunchboxes are not kept in the fridge at nursery, it is recommended to use an insulated box with an ice pack to keep the food safe and cool. Parents should also consult with the child's nursery for any food policies.

question: What is bacterial vaginosis?
answer: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a common cause of unusual vaginal discharge that is not a sexually transmitted infection (STI), but it can increase the risk of getting an STI such as chlamydia.

question: What are the symptoms of bacterial vaginosis?
answer: Symptoms of bacterial vaginosis include an unusual vaginal discharge that has a strong fishy smell, particularly after sex, and a change to the color and consistency of your discharge, such as becoming greyish-white and thin and watery. Half of women with bacterial vaginosis do not have any symptoms.

question: Is bacterial vaginosis serious?
answer: Bacterial vaginosis is not usually serious, but it does need to be treated with antibiotics if you have it. It's also important to seek treatment if you're pregnant as there's a small chance it can cause complications with pregnancy.

question: What causes bacterial vaginosis?
answer: Bacterial vaginosis is caused by a change in the natural balance of bacteria in your vagina, but it is not fully known what causes this to happen. However, you are more likely to get it if you're sexually active, have had a change of partner, have an IUD (contraception device), or use perfumed products in or around your vagina.

question: How is bacterial vaginosis diagnosed?
answer: If you have symptoms of bacterial vaginosis, a GP or sexual health clinic will want to confirm it is bacterial vaginosis and rule out an STI. You'll be asked about your symptoms, and a doctor or nurse may look at your vagina. A cotton bud may be wiped over the discharge inside your vagina to test for bacterial vaginosis and other infections.

question: How is bacterial vaginosis treated?
answer: Bacterial vaginosis is usually treated with antibiotic tablets or gels or creams, which are prescribed by a GP or sexual health clinic. If you have a same-sex partner, they may also need treatment. It's common for bacterial vaginosis to come back, usually within a few months, and if it comes back, you'll usually be given more antibiotics to treat it.

question: What should I do if I think I have bacterial vaginosis?
answer: If you think you have bacterial vaginosis, you should see a GP or go to a sexual health clinic. The condition is not usually serious, but it does need to be treated with antibiotics if you have it. It's also important to seek treatment if you're pregnant as there's a small chance it can cause complications with pregnancy.

question: How can I prevent bacterial vaginosis?
answer: You can help prevent bacterial vaginosis by using water and plain soap to wash your genital area and having showers instead of baths. You should avoid using perfumed soaps, bubble bath, shampoo or shower gel in the bath, and avoid using vaginal deodorants, washes or douches. Additionally, you should not put antiseptic liquids in the bath, use strong detergents to wash your underwear, or smoke.

question: Is bacterial vaginosis an STI?
answer: Bacterial vaginosis is not an STI, even though it can be triggered by sex. A woman can pass it to another woman during sex. You are more likely to get an STI if you have bacterial vaginosis because it makes your vagina less acidic and reduces your natural defenses against infection.

question: Can bacterial vaginosis cause complications during pregnancy?
answer: If you develop bacterial vaginosis in pregnancy, there's a small chance of complications, such as premature birth or miscarriage. But bacterial vaginosis causes no problems in the majority of pregnancies. If you're pregnant and your vaginal discharge changes, you should speak to a GP or your midwife.

question: What is bad breath?
answer: Bad breath, also known as halitosis, is a common condition where unpleasant odors emanate from the mouth.

question: How can one treat bad breath at home?
answer: It is best to keep your mouth, teeth, and tongue clean to ensure there is no bad breath. You can gently brush your teeth and gums at least twice a day for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste, clean your tongue once daily with a tongue scraper or cleaner, clean between your teeth at least once a day with interdental brushes or floss, get regular dental check-ups, and use an antibacterial mouthwash or toothpaste.

question: What are some things to avoid when trying to cure bad breath?
answer: Avoid sugary foods and drinks, smoking, and brushing too hard, so your tongue or gums bleed. Do not rinse your mouth with water immediately after brushing your teeth.

question: What could be the reason for bad breath?
answer: Various reasons result in bad breath. Consumption of strong-smelling food or drink, problems with teeth or gums such as periodontitis, cavities or gum disease, crash dieting, dry mouth, tonsillitis, and acid reflux can cause it, among others.

question: Can sugary foods and drinks lead to bad breath?
answer: Indeed, consuming a lot of sugary food and drink might lead to bad breath.

question: Is it necessary to remove dentures at night?
answer: Yes. Prolonged use of dentures lowers the risk of bad breath. Additionally, keeping them thoroughly cleansed avoids the accumulation of harmful bacteria. Thus, it is advisable to remove them at night to allow your gums to rest.

question: What are the Do's to help treat bad breath?
answer: To treat bad breath, brush your teeth and gums gently at least twice a day for two minutes with fluoride toothpaste, clean your tongue once daily with a tongue scraper or cleaner, clean between your teeth at least once a day with interdental brushes or floss, get regular dental check-ups, keep dentures clean, and use sugar-free mints or chewing gum after having strong-smelling food and drinks.

question: Will using mouthwash or toothpaste help treat bad breath?
answer: Using an antibacterial mouthwash or toothpaste can help fight bad breath by destroying bacteria that cause it.

question: Does bad breath go away on its own?
answer: At times, bad breath resolves on its own or after performing home-based remedies for a few weeks. However, if bad breath persists, it is best to see a dentist.

question: What medical conditions can result in bad breath?
answer: Several medical conditions, including dry mouth, tonsillitis, and acid reflux, might cause bad breath.

question: What is balanitis?
answer: Balanitis is a condition characterized by the swelling and inflammation of the head of the penis. It can also cause soreness and itching, and sometimes a thick discharge or an unpleasant smell.

question: Is balanitis serious?
answer: In most cases, balanitis is not a serious condition. However, it's important to see a GP to find out what's causing it and how to treat it properly.

question: What are the symptoms of balanitis?
answer: The symptoms of balanitis usually include redness, swelling, itchiness, and soreness in the head of the penis. Other symptoms may include pain when peeing, a thick discharge, bleeding around the foreskin, and an unpleasant smell.

question: Where can I get help for balanitis?
answer: If you suspect that you or your child may have balanitis, you should see a GP or go to a sexual health clinic for assessment. Many sexual health clinics offer a walk-in service, where you do not need an appointment.

question: What should I do if I have balanitis?
answer: If you have balanitis, you should wash your penis every day with warm water, pull back your foreskin gently, and dry off afterwards. Refrain from using soap or shower gel, but use an emollient to moisturize the area instead. Additionally, you should choose condoms that are suitable for sensitive skin.

question: What should I do if my child has balanitis?
answer: If your child has balanitis, you should gently wash their penis every day with warm water and dry it off afterwards. Do not use soap, bubble bath or baby wipes, and do not pull your child's foreskin back if it is fixed in place. Change your child's nappies often if they are still in diapers.

question: What are the causes of balanitis?
answer: There are several causes of balanitis, including not washing the penis properly, a tight foreskin, thrush, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and irritants such as soap or condoms. Diabetes may also increase the risk of balanitis.

question: What treatment options are available for balanitis?
answer: Treatment for balanitis depends on the underlying cause, but your GP may prescribe a mild steroid cream or ointment, an antifungal cream or ointment, antibiotics, or, in severe cases, circumcision. If medicine has not helped, circumcision may be considered.

question: Can sexual health clinics help with balanitis?
answer: Yes, sexual health clinics can help with balanitis. They treat problems with the genitals and can conduct tests to identify the underlying cause. Additionally, they often get test results quicker than GP practices.

question: When should I visit a GP if I suspect balanitis?
answer: If you or your child have symptoms of balanitis, or if treatment has not worked, you should see a GP as soon as possible. Additionally, you should visit a GP if the infection is severe or accompanied by thrush, or if you suspect you have diabetes.

question: What are bedbugs?
answer: Bedbugs are small insects that often live on furniture or bedding.

question: What are the signs of bedbugs?
answer: Signs of bedbugs include bites- often on skin exposed while sleeping, spots of blood on your bedding, small brown spots on bedding or furniture.

question: How can I get rid of bedbugs?
answer: If you think you have bedbugs, you should contact your local council or pest control service. It's very difficult to get rid of bedbugs yourself because they can be hard to find and may be resistant to some insecticides.

question: What other information can I find?
answer: You can find your local council on GOV.UK.

question: Is bedwetting in children normal?
answer: Yes, bedwetting in young children is normal. Many children under the age of 5 wet the bed. It can take some time for a child to learn to stay dry throughout the night.

question: What can parents do at home to help with bedwetting?
answer: Parents can give their child enough water to drink during the day, make sure their child goes to the toilet regularly, agree with their child on rewards for positive actions, use waterproof covers on their mattress and duvet, and make sure they have easy access to a toilet at night.

question: Is it okay to punish a child for bedwetting?
answer: No, punishing a child for bedwetting is not okay. It is not their fault and can make bedwetting worse.

question: What drinks should parents avoid giving their child if they wet the bed?
answer: Parents should avoid giving their child drinks containing caffeine, such as cola, tea and coffee, as this can make them pee more.

question: When should I see a GP regarding my child's bedwetting?
answer: You should see a GP if you have tried things you can do at home and your child keeps wetting the bed, or if your child has started wetting the bed again after being dry for more than 6 months.

question: What treatments can a GP suggest for a child who wets the bed?
answer: If a child keeps wetting the bed, a GP can suggest options such as a bedwetting alarm or medicine to reduce how much pee your child makes at night. The GP will check if treatment is helping and offer support if you are finding it hard to cope.

question: What are the causes of bedwetting?
answer: There are many reasons why a child might wet the bed, including not feeling the need to pee while sleeping, making too much pee at night and stress at home or at school. Bedwetting may also be caused by an underlying health condition such as diabetes or constipation.

question: Can bedwetting be genetic?
answer: Yes, bedwetting can be genetic and often runs in families.

question: Should parents wake their child at night to use the toilet?
answer: No, parents should not regularly wake or carry their child in the night to use the toilet, as this will not help in the long term.

question: Are there any resources or organizations that can provide more information and advice on bedwetting?
answer: Yes, Bladder and Bowel UK and ERIC provide resources for children and young people with bladder problems, including bedwetting.

question: What is Bell's palsy?
answer: Bell's palsy is a temporary weakness or lack of movement affecting 1 side of the face. Unlike a stroke, the facial weakness develops gradually.

question: What are the symptoms of a stroke?
answer: The symptoms of a stroke usually come on suddenly and may include face drooping on 1 side, an inability to lift up both arms and keep them there, and difficulty speaking.

question: What are the non-urgent symptoms of Bell's palsy?
answer: Non-urgent symptoms of Bell's palsy include weakness or total paralysis on 1 side of your face that develops quickly within 72 hours, a drooping eyelid or corner of the mouth, drooling, a dry mouth, a loss of taste, and eye irritation.

question: What should I do if I experience signs of a stroke?
answer: You should call 999 immediately if you experience signs of a stroke, such as face drooping on 1 side, an inability to lift up both arms and keep them there, and difficulty speaking.

question: What should I do if I experience non-urgent symptoms of Bell's palsy?
answer: If you experience non-urgent symptoms of Bell's palsy, you should see your GP as soon as possible. Treatment for Bell's palsy is more effective if started early (within 72 hours).

question: Is Bell's palsy common in children?
answer: Bell's palsy is rare in children. Most children who are affected make a full recovery without treatment.

question: What kind of treatment is available for Bell's palsy?
answer: Treatments for Bell's palsy include a 10-day course of steroid medicine, eyedrops and eye ointment to stop the affected eye drying out and surgical tape to keep the eye closed at bedtime. The GP might prescribe a type of steroid called prednisolone, which should begin within 3 days (72 hours) of the symptoms starting.

question: How long does Bell's palsy usually last?
answer: Most people make a full recovery within 9 months, but it can take longer. In a small number of cases, the facial weakness can be permanent.

question: Can Bell's palsy be prevented?
answer: Bell's palsy cannot usually be prevented because it's probably caused by an infection. It may be linked to the herpes virus.

question: What should I do if living with Bell's palsy is affecting my mental health?
answer: If living with Bell's palsy is affecting your mental health, you should speak to a GP.

question: What is a benign brain tumor?
answer: A benign brain tumor is a mass of cells that grows relatively slowly in the brain. It is non-cancerous and tends to stay in one place, not spreading to other parts of the body.

question: What are the types and grades of non-cancerous brain tumors?
answer: There are many different types of non-cancerous brain tumors, including gliomas, meningiomas, acoustic neuromas, craniopharyngiomas, haemangioblastomas, and pituitary adenomas. Non-cancerous brain tumors are graded from 1 to 2 according to how fast they grow and spread, and how likely they are to grow back after treatment.

question: What are the symptoms of non-cancerous brain tumors?
answer: The symptoms of a non-cancerous brain tumor depend on how big it is and where it is in the brain. Common symptoms include persistent headaches, seizures, feeling sick all the time, changes in personality, weakness or paralysis, vision problems, or speech problems.

question: When should I see a GP if I have symptoms of a brain tumor?
answer: If you have symptoms of a brain tumor, it is important to see a GP. While it is unlikely to be a tumor, these symptoms need to be assessed by a doctor. The GP will examine you, ask about your symptoms, and may test your nervous system. If the GP thinks you may have a brain tumor, or they're not sure what's causing your symptoms, they'll refer you to a brain and nerve specialist called a neurologist.

question: How are non-cancerous brain tumors treated?
answer: The treatment for non-cancerous brain tumors depends on the type and location of the tumor. Surgery is used to remove most non-cancerous brain tumors, and they do not usually come back after being removed. If all of the tumor cannot be removed, other treatments such as radiotherapy and chemotherapy may be needed to control the growth of the remaining abnormal cells.

question: What is the difference between benign and malignant brain tumors?
answer: A benign brain tumor is non-cancerous, meaning it tends to stay in one place and does not spread to other parts of the body, while a malignant brain tumor is cancerous and can grow quickly, invade nearby tissue, and spread to other parts of the brain or body.

question: What is the likelihood of a non-cancerous brain tumor growing back after treatment?
answer: Non-cancerous brain tumors tend to stay in one place and do not spread. It will not usually come back if all of the tumor can be safely removed during surgery. If the tumor cannot be completely removed, there's a risk it could grow back. In this case, it'll be closely monitored using scans or treated with radiotherapy.

question: What support is available for people with non-cancerous brain tumors?
answer: The Brain Tumour Charity has links to support groups in the UK, and Brain Tumour Research also has details of helplines you can contact. Speaking to a counsellor can also help with the emotional aspects of the diagnosis and treatment.

question: What is bird flu?
answer: Bird flu, or avian flu, is a type of influenza that spreads among birds but it can also affect humans in rare cases. There are 4 strains of bird flu that have caused concern in recent years, namely H5N1, H7N9, H5N6, and H5N8.

question: How does bird flu spread to humans?
answer: Bird flu is mostly spread by close contact with an infected bird, whether dead or alive. This includes touching infected birds or their droppings, killing or preparing infected poultry for cooking, or visiting markets where live birds are sold. It is important to be careful and avoid such contacts.

question: What should I do to prevent bird flu when visiting a foreign country with an outbreak?
answer: If you are visiting a foreign country that has an outbreak of bird flu, you should wash your hands often with warm water and soap, especially before and after handling food, use different utensils for cooked and raw meat, make sure meat is cooked until steaming hot, and avoid contact with live birds and poultry. You should also avoid visiting live animal markets or poultry farms and refrain from bringing live birds or poultry into the UK.

question: Can I catch bird flu through eating fully cooked poultry or eggs?
answer: No, you cannot catch bird flu through eating fully cooked poultry or eggs, even in areas with an outbreak of bird flu.

question: What are the symptoms of bird flu in humans?
answer: The main symptoms of bird flu in humans include a very high temperature or feeling hot or shivery, aching muscles, headache, a cough or shortness of breath, as well as other symptoms such as diarrhea, sickness, stomach pain, chest pain, bleeding from the nose and gums, or conjunctivitis. It usually takes 3 to 5 days for the first symptoms to appear after you have been infected.

question: What should I do if I suspect I have bird flu and have recently visited an affected area?
answer: If you suspect you have bird flu and have recently visited an affected area, you should use NHS 111 online or call NHS 111 for advice. If you are abroad, seek medical help straight away, and contact your travel insurance company if you need advice about where to get help. You should also inform your doctor about your recent travel and other relevant information, such as having been in close contact with infected birds or people.

question: Is there a vaccine for bird flu?
answer: No, there is currently no vaccine for bird flu, and the seasonal flu vaccine does not protect against bird flu.

question: What happens if bird flu is suspected in birds?
answer: If bird flu is suspected in poultry, other captive birds, or wild birds, it must be reported immediately by calling the relevant authority. This is because bird flu is a notifiable disease in poultry and other captive birds. Reporting infected birds can help the authorities keep track of the spread of the disease, and help to prevent its spread.

question: What tests are done to confirm bird flu in humans?
answer: To confirm bird flu in humans, the doctor may do a nose and throat swab to see if they contain the virus, or test any coughed-up phlegm for the virus. If the tests are normal, it is unlikely that you have bird flu.

question: What is the treatment for bird flu in humans?
answer: If you are suspected of having bird flu, you will be advised to stay at home or will be cared for in hospital in isolation from other patients. You may be given antiviral medicine such as oseltamivir (Tamiflu) or zanamivir (Relenza) to reduce the severity of the condition, prevent complications, and improve your chances of survival. Antiviral medicines are also sometimes given to people who have been in close contact with infected birds or people, such as family or healthcare staff.

question: What are birthmarks?
answer: Birthmarks are coloured marks on the skin that are present at birth or soon afterwards.

question: Do all birthmarks require treatment?
answer: Most birthmarks are harmless and disappear without treatment, but some may need to be treated.

question: What are strawberry marks?
answer: Strawberry marks are raised red lumps that appear soon after birth. They usually get bigger for the first 6 to 12 months, and then shrink and disappear by the age of 7. They may need treatment if they affect vision, breathing, or feeding.

question: What are congenital moles?
answer: Congenital moles are brown or black moles caused by an overgrowth of pigment cells in the skin. They may develop into skin cancer if they're large (the risk increases the larger they are) but do not need to be treated unless there's a risk of skin cancer.

question: What are the possible treatments for birthmarks?
answer: Possible treatments for birthmarks include medicines, laser therapy, and surgery. Medicines are used to reduce blood flow to the birthmark, which can slow down its growth and make it lighter in colour. Laser therapy works best if started between 6 months and 1 year of age, where heat and light are used to make the birthmark smaller and lighter. Surgery is used to remove the birthmark but can leave scarring. A birthmark can be removed on the NHS if it's affecting a person's health. If you want a birthmark removed for cosmetic reasons, you'll have to pay to have it done privately.

question: What is a black eye?
answer: A black eye is bruising and swelling around your eye, usually caused by a blow to the area, such as a punch or fall.

question: How long does it take for a black eye to heal?
answer: A black eye should get better within 2 to 3 weeks.

question: What can I do to ease a black eye myself?
answer: You can gently hold an ice pack (or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a cloth) to the area around your eye for about 10 to 20 minutes at a time, and repeat regularly during the first 1 to 2 days. You can also take painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen for any pain. After the first 2 days, gently apply a warm (not hot) heat pack or cloth to the area around your eye regularly during the day.

question: What should I avoid doing if I have a black eye?
answer: You should not take aspirin, unless prescribed by a doctor, as this can make the bruising worse. You should also not press or rub the area around your eye and not put ice directly on your skin.

question: When should I ask for an urgent GP appointment or call 111?
answer: You should ask for an urgent GP appointment or call 111 if you have severe pain or swelling, have a headache that does not go away, or blurry vision, the area around your eye is warm or leaking pus, your temperature is very high, or you feel hot and shivery, you're taking blood-thinning medicine (such as warfarin), or you have a bleeding disorder (such as haemophilia).

question: When should I go to A&E if I have a black eye?
answer: You should go to A&E if there's blood visible in your eye, you have an irregularly shaped pupil (the black dot at the centre of the eye), you had a blow to the head and have bruising around both eyes, you have problems with your vision, such as double vision, loss of vision, seeing flashing light, halos or shadows, or pain when looking at a bright light, or you cannot move your eye.

question: What kind of painkillers can I take for a black eye?
answer: You can take painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen for any pain.

question: Is it safe to put ice directly on the skin if I have a black eye?
answer: No, you should not put ice directly on your skin.

question: What are the signs that I might be bleeding from the bottom?
answer: You might be bleeding from the bottom if you have blood on your toilet paper, red streaks on the outside of your poo, pink water in the toilet bowl, blood in your poo, or bloody diarrhea. Very dark, smelly poo can also be a sign of bleeding from the bottom.

question: Is bleeding from the bottom always a serious issue?
answer: A small amount of one-off bleeding from the bottom is not usually a serious problem. However, if you're experiencing any of the symptoms mentioned, it's best to get checked by a GP.

question: When should I see a GP for rectal bleeding?
answer: You should see a GP if you notice blood in your poo, you've had blood in your poo for three weeks, your poo has been softer, thinner or longer than normal for three weeks, you're in a lot of pain around the bottom, or if you have a pain or lump in your tummy. You should also see a GP if your child has blood in their poo.

question: What should I do if I'm experiencing non-stop bleeding?
answer: If you're bleeding non-stop or if there's a lot of blood, such as the toilet water turning red or seeing large blood clots, then you should go to A&E or call 999 immediately.

question: What are the common causes of bright red blood on toilet paper or poo streaks?
answer: Bright red blood on toilet paper or poo streaks can be caused by eating a lot of red or purple foods like tomatoes and beetroot. But it can also be a sign of something else, so it's best to check with a GP if you're worried.

question: How can I prepare for a GP appointment if I'm experiencing bleeding from the bottom?
answer: It might be helpful to write down any symptoms you've been experiencing, how long you've had them, and whether they've been getting worse or better. Try to remember to bring a sample of poo for testing, too.

question: What will a GP do to determine the cause of my rectal bleeding?
answer: A GP may perform a rectal examination by checking your bottom with a gloved finger, ask for a sample of poo for testing, and refer you to a specialist for further tests if necessary.

question: Can taking iron tablets or eating certain foods cause dark or black-colored poo?
answer: Yes, taking iron tablets or eating a lot of dark-colored foods like liquorice and blueberries can make poo appear very dark or black. But it's best to ask a GP to do a test to confirm that there's no underlying issue.

question: How can I differentiate between bright red blood and dark blood in my poo?
answer: Bright red blood on toilet paper or poo streaks is usually a sign of bleeding closer to the anus, while dark-colored poo or blood usually suggests that the bleeding has occurred further up the digestive tract.

question: Why is it important to check for bowel cancer if one is bleeding from the bottom?
answer: Bleeding from the bottom is sometimes a sign of bowel cancer, which is easier to treat if detected early. Therefore, if you experience any symptoms of rectal bleeding, it is essential to get them checked out by a GP.

question: What is blepharitis?
answer: Blepharitis is a condition that causes swollen, itchy eyelids. It's not usually serious and can often be treated by washing your eyelids every day.

question: What are the symptoms of blepharitis?
answer: Symptoms of blepharitis include sore eyelids, itchy eyes, a gritty feeling in the eyes, flakes or crusts around the roots of the eyelashes, and eyelids sticking together in the morning when you wake up.

question: Can blepharitis be spread to other people?
answer: No, blepharitis cannot be spread to other people.

question: How can I check if I have blepharitis?
answer: If you experience sore eyelids, itchy eyes, a gritty feeling in the eyes, flakes or crusts around the roots of the eyelashes, and eyelids sticking together in the morning when you wake up, you may be experiencing blepharitis. However, it's always best to consult a medical professional to confirm the diagnosis.

question: What can I do to treat and prevent blepharitis?
answer: You can clean your eyelids twice a day to start with and then once a day as your symptoms improve. It's important to continue to clean your eyes, even if your symptoms clear up. Additionally, you should avoid wearing contact lenses and using eye makeup, especially eyeliner and mascara while you have symptoms.

question: How do I clean my eyes if I have blepharitis?
answer: To clean your eyes if you have blepharitis, soak a clean flannel or cotton wool in warm water and place it on your closed eyelid for 5 to 10 minutes. Gently massage your eyelids for around 30 seconds then clean your eyelids using cotton wool or a cotton bud. It might help to use a small amount of baby shampoo in water. Gently wipe along the edge of your eyelids to remove any flakes or crusts.

question: Can a pharmacist help with treating blepharitis?
answer: Yes, a pharmacist might be able to suggest things to help keep your eyelids clean, including eye pads and wipes, and eyedrops. It's important to consult with a pharmacist or medical professional before trying any new treatments.

question: When should I see a GP for blepharitis?
answer: If your blepharitis symptoms do not improve after a few weeks of cleaning your eyelids or if you have severe symptoms or other eye-related issues, you should see a GP for a proper diagnosis and treatment.

question: What treatments might a GP recommend for blepharitis?
answer: A GP might suggest using an antibiotic cream or ointment that you rub on your eyelid if your blepharitis symptoms do not clear up after cleaning your eyelids regularly. If blepharitis has caused other problems, such as a lump of fluid under the skin (cyst), antibiotic eyedrops or tablets may be recommended. In severe cases or if you have other eye symptoms, the GP may refer you to an eye specialist (ophthalmologist).

question: What causes blepharitis?
answer: Blepharitis can be caused by a type of bacteria that lives on the skin, a skin condition such as seborrhoeic dermatitis, or the glands inside the eyelids not producing enough oil.

question: How long does it take for blisters to heal on their own?
answer: Blisters often heal on their own within a week.

question: What is the best way to treat blisters myself?
answer: To protect the blister and prevent infection, you should cover it with a soft plaster or padded dressing, wash your hands before touching a burst blister, and allow the fluid in a burst blister to drain before covering it.

question: Can I burst a blister myself?
answer: No, you should not burst a blister yourself as this can increase the risk of infection.

question: What should I do if I have an infected blister?
answer: You should not ignore an infected blister as it could lead to a skin or blood infection. See a doctor for medical attention immediately.

question: What can a pharmacist recommend for blisters?
answer: A pharmacist can recommend a plaster or dressing to cover the blister while it heals. A hydrocolloid dressing (a moist dressing) can protect the blister, reduce pain and speed up healing.

question: What causes blisters and how can I prevent them?
answer: Blisters develop to protect the damaged skin and mostly occur due to friction, burns, and skin reactions. To prevent it, wear comfortable, well-fitting shoes, wear new shoes for short periods of time, wear thick socks during exercise, dust talcum powder in your socks if you get sweaty feet, and wear protective gloves when you exercise or use tools at work.

question: When should I seek medical help for blisters?
answer: You should seek medical help if a blister was caused by a burn or scald, sunburn, an allergic reaction, or by a medical condition such as chickenpox, cold sores, genital herpes, bullous impetigo, pompholyx, scabies or hand, foot and mouth disease.

question: How can a GP help with blisters?
answer: A GP can burst a large or painful blister using a sterilized needle and prescribe antibiotics if the blister is infected. They can also offer treatment and advice if blisters are caused by a medical condition.

question: What is bloating?
answer: Bloating is a feeling of fullness and discomfort in the stomach, which is very common. There are various ways to alleviate bloating but it is advised to consult a doctor if it is persistent.

question: What are the symptoms of bloating?
answer: Symptoms of bloating include a full or enlarged stomach, discomfort or pain in the stomach, rumbling or gurgling noises in the stomach, and increased flatulence.

question: What are the causes of bloating?
answer: Bloating is primarily caused by excessive gas in the digestive tract which can result from eating certain foods, swallowing air, or problems with digestion. Some medical conditions such as constipation, coeliac disease, and irritable bowel syndrome can also lead to bloating.

question: Can bloating be a sign of ovarian cancer?
answer: Bloating that does not go away can be a sign of a more serious condition like ovarian cancer. It is recommended to consult with a doctor if bloating persists.

question: What measures can be taken to reduce bloating?
answer: Ways to reduce bloating include regular exercise, drinking water, avoiding carbonated drinks, and eating smaller, more frequent meals. Furthermore, keeping the mouth closed to avoid swallowing air and chewing food correctly can also help.

question: What foods should be avoided to prevent bloating?
answer: Foods that are known to cause gas such as beans, lentils, and cabbage should be avoided to prevent bloating. Additionally, processed, sugary, fatty, and spicy foods should also be consumed in moderation.

question: Can pharmacists help with bloating?
answer: Pharmacists can provide assistance with bloating by suggesting medications such as laxatives and medicines like Buscopan to ease the discomfort.

question: When should I see a GP for bloating?
answer: You should see a doctor if bloating persists for three weeks or more, occurs regularly (more than 12 times a month) and is not relieved through lifestyle changes. Additionally, it is recommended to consult a doctor in case of other symptoms like a swelling or lump in the stomach, being sick, diarrhoea, constipation, weight loss, or blood in the stool.

question: What should I do if I have severe stomach pain?
answer: If you experience sudden severe stomach pain, call 999 or go to A&E immediately. Other symptoms include a tender stomach or pain upon touch, blood in vomit or urine, black stools, and difficulty breathing or chest pains.

question: What treatment options are available for bloating?
answer: Most cases of bloating do not require treatment. If treatment is deemed necessary, it would depend on the cause of bloating. A general practitioner may suggest seeing an NHS dietitian to create a personalized diet plan or refer a specialist for further testing.

question: What are the symptoms of a blood clot?
answer: Symptoms of a blood clot include throbbing or cramping pain, swelling, redness and warmth in a leg or arm. Sudden breathlessness, sharp chest pain (may be worse when you breathe in) and a cough or coughing up blood.

question: How can I prevent blood clots?
answer: You can help avoid clots by staying active – taking regular walks can help, drinking plenty of water to avoid dehydration, and wearing flight stockings or flight socks to improve your blood flow on long flights. Avoid sitting for long periods without moving and don't drink lots of alcohol or smoke.

question: Who is at a higher risk of getting blood clots?
answer: People who are staying in or recently left the hospital, are overweight, smoke, use combined hormonal contraception, have had a blood clot before, are pregnant or have just had a baby, and have an inflammatory condition such as Crohn's disease or rheumatoid arthritis are at higher risk of getting blood clots.

question: What should I do if I think I have a blood clot?
answer: Get advice from 111 now if you think you have a blood clot. They can arrange a phone call from a nurse or doctor if you need one. Call 999 or go to A&E immediately if you're struggling to breathe or someone has passed out.

question: What is a blood clot in a leg called?
answer: A blood clot in a leg is called a DVT (deep vein thrombosis).

question: What should I do if I'm at a high risk of blood clots?
answer: If you're at a high risk of blood clots, follow the advice of your care team about preventing clots. This may involve wearing stockings that improve your blood flow or taking medicine to reduce the risk of clots (anticoagulants).

question: Can a blood clot be life-threatening?
answer: Yes, blood clots can be life-threatening if not treated quickly. It’s important to get medical attention immediately if you suspect a blood clot.

question: What are the causes of blood clots?
answer: Blood clots may be caused by factors such as obesity, smoking, pregnancy, and certain medications like hormonal birth control. People who are hospitalized or immobile for prolonged periods of time are also at higher risk.

question: What are some other ways to get help with blood clots?
answer: You can also ask your GP practice for an urgent appointment if you think you have a blood clot. They may be able to help you or refer you to a specialist if needed.

question: What are some things that increase the risk of blood clots?
answer: Aside from the factors previously mentioned, other things that increase the risk of blood clots include cancer, heart disease, a family history of blood clots, and certain genetic disorders.

question: What are the four main blood groups?
answer: The four main blood groups are A, B, AB, and O.

question: What determines your blood group?
answer: Your blood group is determined by the genes you inherit from your parents.

question: What are antibodies in the blood?
answer: Antibodies are proteins found in plasma that recognize foreign substances, such as germs, and alert your immune system, which destroys them.

question: What are antigens in the blood?
answer: Antigens are protein molecules found on the surface of red blood cells.

question: What is the ABO system of blood group classification?
answer: The ABO system is a classification system that defines the four main blood groups based on the presence or absence of antigens on red blood cells.

question: What is the most common blood group?
answer: The most common blood group is O, with almost half of the UK population (48%) having it.

question: Why can receiving blood from the wrong ABO group be life-threatening?
answer: Receiving blood from the wrong ABO group can be life-threatening because if the body's immune system detects foreign antigens on the red blood cells, it can react with the antibodies, resulting in destruction of red blood cells and potentially leading to serious health problems, including death.

question: What is the Rh system of blood group classification?
answer: The Rh system is a classification system that defines the presence or absence of an antigen known as the RhD antigen on red blood cells, resulting in either RhD-positive or RhD-negative blood type.

question: What happens during a blood group test?
answer: During a blood group test, your red blood cells are mixed with different antibody solutions to identify your blood group.

question: Who can donate blood?
answer: Most people who are fit and healthy, weigh at least 50kg, and are between 17-66 years old (or over 70 if they've given blood before) can donate blood.

question: What is blood in semen?
answer: Blood in semen refers to the presence of blood in the semen. It can be bright red, pink, brown or reddish-brown and often goes away on its own.

question: Should I see a doctor if I have blood in my semen?
answer: Yes, it is important to get it checked by a GP to make sure it's not a sign of something serious.

question: What are the common causes of blood in semen?
answer: Common causes of blood in semen include infections, recent procedures or tests, and problems with the prostate.

question: Is blood in semen always a sign of cancer?
answer: No, blood in semen is usually not a sign of cancer, but it can be in rare cases.

question: What symptoms may accompany blood in semen?
answer: Depending on the cause, you may also have other symptoms like blood in your pee, pain when peeing or peeing more often than usual.

question: How is blood in semen diagnosed?
answer: A GP can check for common causes and refer you to a specialist for more tests if needed.

question: Do I need treatment for blood in semen?
answer: Blood in semen does not usually need to be treated. It often goes away by itself in a few days or weeks. If a cause can be found, this may need to be treated.

question: What tests may be done to diagnose the cause of blood in semen?
answer: Tests that may be done include urine and blood tests, ultrasound, and biopsy.

question: Can blood in semen be prevented?
answer: Preventing blood in semen depends on the underlying cause. Practicing safe sex and good hygiene can help reduce the risk of infections.

question: Is blood in semen always serious?
answer: Blood in semen is not usually caused by something serious, but it should still be checked by a doctor to rule out potential health concerns.

question: What should I do if I have blood in my urine?
answer: You must get it checked out by a GP. Ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 if you have blood in your pee, even if it's the first time it's happened, there's only a small amount of blood, or you're not sure it's blood.

question: Is blood in urine usually a sign of something serious?
answer: No, blood in urine is not usually caused by anything serious, but it must be checked out by a GP because it can also be a sign of cancer. This is easier to treat if it's found early.

question: What color can blood in urine be?
answer: Blood in your pee may be bright pink, red or dark brown.

question: What can a GP do if I have blood in my urine?
answer: If you have blood in your pee, a GP will ask about your symptoms and may need to check inside your bottom (rectal examination), and your vagina if you're a woman. They might also ask for a pee sample or arrange a blood test, prescribe antibiotics if they think you have an infection, or refer you to a specialist for tests.

question: Is blood in urine always a sign of cancer?
answer: No, blood in urine is not always a sign of cancer, but it should be checked out by a GP because it can also be a sign of other conditions like kidney stones, urinary tract infections, or an enlarged prostate.

question: Can eating beetroot or taking new medicine cause blood in urine?
answer: Yes, eating beetroot can turn your pee pink, and some medicines can turn pee red or brown. Therefore, blood in urine may not always be blood, so it's important to see a GP if you think it's blood in your pee.

question: What tests might a specialist use to diagnose blood in urine?
answer: A specialist might use various tests to diagnose blood in urine, such as a cystoscopy, which involves looking inside your bladder with a thin tube and a camera, a CT scan, or an MRI.

question: Is blood in urine more common in certain people or age groups?
answer: Blood in urine can happen to anyone, but it's more common in men over 50, and it can also occur in women from time to time.

question: How is cancer detected if I have blood in my urine?
answer: If cancer is suspected, a GP or specialist will usually recommend further tests to diagnose it. These might include a biopsy of your bladder, kidneys or prostate to check for cancer cells or abnormal growth, or imaging tests to see inside your urinary tract.

question: Can blood in my urine go away on its own?
answer: Blood in urine can go away on its own if it's caused by a mild condition like a urinary tract infection or injury, but it's important to see a GP to rule out more serious conditions like cancer. If left untreated, these conditions can become more severe and difficult to treat.

question: What is a blood transfusion?
answer: A blood transfusion is a medical procedure in which an individual receives blood from a donor. The procedure is safe and can be lifesaving.

question: Why might someone need a blood transfusion?
answer: A blood transfusion may be needed if an individual has a shortage of red blood cells due to various conditions such as sickle cell disease, thalassaemia, cancer, cancer treatments, or severe bleeding resulting from surgery, childbirth, or a serious accident.

question: How is it determined what blood type an individual has?
answer: Before the transfusion, a sample of the individual's blood will be taken to check their blood group. They will only be given blood that is safe for their blood group.

question: What happens during a blood transfusion?
answer: During a blood transfusion, the individual sits or lies down in a chair or bed, and a needle is inserted into a vein in their arm or hand. The needle is connected to a tube and a bag of blood. The blood runs through the tube into the vein. It usually takes up to 4 hours to receive 1 bag of blood.

question: What are the possible side effects of a blood transfusion?
answer: Possible side effects include a sharp prick during needle insertion, followed by fever, chills, or rash during the transfusion. These effects can usually be treated with paracetamol or a slowed transfusion. The individual may also experience arm or hand aches and bruises for a few days after.

question: How can someone reduce their risk of needing a blood transfusion?
answer: If possible, an individual can take medicine such as tranexamic acid to lower the risk of bleeding, or iron tablets or injections to boost the number of red blood cells, which can decrease the chances of needing a blood transfusion.

question: What should someone do if they feel unwell after a blood transfusion?
answer: If an individual feels unwell within 24 hours of having a blood transfusion, especially if they have difficulty breathing or pain in their chest or back, they should contact their doctor or nurse right away.

question: How safe are blood transfusions?
answer: Blood transfusions are common and very safe procedures. All donor blood is checked before use to make sure they don't contain serious infections such as hepatitis or HIV. There's only a very small risk of complications like an allergic reaction to the donor blood or problems with the heart, lungs, or immune system.

question: What alternatives are there to a blood transfusion?
answer: A blood transfusion will only be recommended if it's necessary and other treatments will not help. If an individual is at risk of needing a blood transfusion, they may be given medicine such as tranexamic acid or iron tablets or injections, which can reduce the chances of a blood transfusion.

question: Can someone give blood after having a blood transfusion?
answer: Currently, an individual who had a blood transfusion after 1 January 1980 cannot donate blood as a precautionary measure to reduce the risk of a serious condition called variant CJD (vCJD) being passed on by donors.

question: What is blushing and why is it a problem?
answer: Blushing is a natural response to feeling hot, anxious, or embarrassed. However, if it happens frequently, it can be embarrassing and affect your day-to-day life, causing undue stress and discomfort.

question: What are some things that can help stop blushing?
answer: Some things that can help stop blushing include doing breathing exercises to reduce stress and anxiety, keeping cool by removing a layer of clothing and drinking water, and wearing makeup that can help reduce redness in stressful situations.

question: What are some things that can trigger blushing?
answer: Blushing is often triggered by feelings of embarrassment, anxiety, or feeling hot. It can also be a symptom of certain medical conditions or a side effect of some medications.

question: Can spicy foods or hot drinks cause blushing?
answer: Yes, spicy foods and hot drinks can cause blushing in some people. If you are prone to blushing, it may be best to avoid these types of foods and beverages.

question: What can I do if my blushing is affecting my everyday life?
answer: If your blushing is affecting your everyday life, you should make an appointment with your GP. They can help determine the cause of your blushing and suggest appropriate treatments.

question: What are some treatments for blushing that my GP might suggest?
answer: Treatments for blushing will depend on the cause. Your GP may suggest a talking therapy like cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) if your blushing is caused by stress or anxiety, or medicines to help reduce anxiety or treat an underlying medical condition.

question: Can surgical treatment be an option for severe blushing?
answer: Very rarely, surgery may be an option if blushing is severe and other treatments have not helped. However, it's important to note that surgery can cause serious and long-lasting side effects.

question: Can medication help reduce blushing?
answer: Yes, medication can help reduce blushing. Your GP may suggest taking medication to help reduce anxiety or treat an underlying medical condition that is causing your blushing.

question: What else besides blushing may be a symptom of certain medical conditions?
answer: Besides blushing, certain medical conditions may also cause hot flashes, sweating, and feelings of anxiety or panic.

question: Is it important to check the side effects of my medication for blushing?
answer: Yes, it's important to check the side effects of any medications you are taking to see if blushing is listed. If you suspect that your medication is causing your blushing, you should talk to your GP.

question: What is body dysmorphic disorder (BDD)?
answer: Body dysmorphic disorder, or body dysmorphia, is a mental health condition where a person spends a lot of time worrying about flaws in their appearance. These flaws are often unnoticeable to others.

question: Can BDD affect your daily life?
answer: Yes, BDD can seriously affect your daily life, including your work, social life and relationships. It can also lead to depression, self-harm and even thoughts of suicide.

question: How can I get help for BDD?
answer: You should see a GP if you think you might have BDD. They'll probably ask a number of questions about your symptoms and how they affect your life. You may be treated by the GP, or they may refer you to a mental health specialist for further assessment and treatment.

question: What treatments are available for BDD?
answer: The symptoms of BDD can get better with treatment. If your symptoms are relatively mild, you should be referred for a type of talking therapy called cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which you have either on your own or in a group. If you have moderate symptoms, you should be offered either CBT or a type of antidepressant medicine called a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). If your symptoms are more severe, or other treatments do not work, you should be offered CBT together with an SSRI.

question: What is cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT)?
answer: CBT can help you manage your BDD symptoms by changing the way you think and behave. It helps you learn what triggers your symptoms, and teaches you different ways of thinking about and dealing with your habits. CBT for treating BDD will usually include a technique known as exposure and response prevention (ERP). This involves gradually facing situations that would normally make you think obsessively about your appearance and feel anxious. Your therapist will help you to find other ways of dealing with your feelings in these situations so that, over time, you become able to deal with them without feeling self-conscious or afraid.

question: What are selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)?
answer: SSRIs are a type of antidepressant. There are a number of different SSRIs, but fluoxetine is most commonly used to treat BDD. It may take up to 12 weeks for SSRIs to have an effect on your BDD symptoms.

question: What can I do to help with BDD?
answer: Some people may find it helpful to contact or join a support group for information, advice and practical tips on coping with BDD. Practising mindfulness exercises may help you if you're feeling low or anxious. Some people also find it helpful to get together with friends or family, or to try doing something new to improve their mental wellbeing. It may also be helpful to try some relaxation and breathing exercises to relieve stress and anxiety.

question: What is a boil?
answer: A boil is a hard and painful lump that fills with pus. Most boils go away on their own, but if you keep getting them or have a long-term condition such as diabetes, you should see a GP for treatment.

question: What can I do to help a boil?
answer: You can soak a flannel in warm water and hold it against the boil for 10 minutes 4 times a day, clean the area around the boil with antibacterial soap if pus comes out, cover the area with a dressing or gauze until it heals, bathe or shower every day and wash your hands regularly, take paracetamol or ibuprofen to ease the pain, and wash your towels and bedding at least once a week at a high temperature.

question: What should I do if I have a boil on my face?
answer: You should see a GP for treatment if you have a boil on your face, a group of boils (carbuncle), a long-term condition such as diabetes, or if you've had a boil for 2 weeks and the things you've tried are not helping.

question: What should I avoid doing if I have a boil?
answer: You should not share your towel with other people, and you should not go to a swimming pool or gym until the boil has gone, as you could pass the infection on to others.

question: How can I prevent getting boils?
answer: You can try to prevent getting boils by washing your hands regularly, avoiding close contact with someone else who has boils, and being careful when shaving to avoid cutting your skin.

question: What are carbuncles?
answer: Carbuncles are less common than boils and mostly affect middle-aged men. They are a group of boils that are usually located on the back of the neck, shoulders, or thighs.

question: What treatments are available for boils?
answer: A GP can check if you need treatment for boils. You may need a small procedure to drain the boil to get rid of the pus or antibiotics.

question: Can weight affect my likelihood of getting boils?
answer: Yes, if you are very overweight and have folds of skin, you may be more likely to get boils in those areas. Losing weight may help prevent boils from forming.

question: Can I take the bowel cancer screening test if I have haemorrhoids?
answer: Yes, you can still take the bowel cancer screening test even if you have haemorrhoids. However, it is more likely that you will get a result that requires further testing due to blood from your haemorrhoids or polyps/cancer. If blood is found in your sample, you will be offered another test called colonoscopy to look for the cause.

question: Can I assist someone I care for in taking the home testing kit for bowel cancer screening?
answer: Yes, you can help someone you care for with the home testing kit for bowel cancer screening if they give you permission and understand the screening process. If the person does not have the capacity to give their consent or understand the process, you should speak to their GP for advice.

question: Is it possible to use the home testing kit if I have had bowel surgery?
answer: Yes, you can use the home testing kit if you have a working bowel. However, if you have had surgery to remove all of your bowel or you have a stoma bag, screening may not be helpful. If you are not sure if screening is suitable for you, it is advisable to check with a GP or call the free bowel cancer screening helpline.

question: Do private healthcare providers offer screening for bowel cancer?
answer: Yes, private healthcare providers offer bowel cancer screening, but it is not the same as the NHS screening. The NHS programme provides care for you through the whole screening process, including further treatment and care that you might need. With private screening, the care you may need following screening may not be available from the provider.

question: What will happen if blood is found in my poo sample during the bowel cancer screening test?
answer: If blood is found in your poo sample during the bowel cancer screening test, you will be offered another test called colonoscopy to look for the cause. This may be caused by your haemorrhoids or it could be due to polyps or cancer.

question: Is bowel cancer screening compulsory?
answer: No, bowel cancer screening is not compulsory, but it is strongly recommended by the NHS for people aged 50 to 74 years old.

question: What should I do if I do not receive the bowel cancer screening kit?
answer: If you are eligible for the bowel cancer screening kit but you haven't received one, contact the bowel cancer screening helpline on 0800 707 60 60.

question: Do I need to change my diet before taking the home testing kit for bowel cancer screening?
answer: There is no need to change your diet before taking the home testing kit for bowel cancer screening. However, you should avoid certain foods and medications that can affect the test results, such as red meat, vitamin C supplements, and aspirin.

question: Will the bowel cancer screening test hurt?
answer: No, the bowel cancer screening test is not painful. You will be provided with instructions on how to collect a small sample of your poo in a specially designed container.

question: What happens after I take the bowel cancer screening test?
answer: After you take the bowel cancer screening test, you will receive your results within 2 weeks. If your test is normal, you will be invited for screening again in 2 years' time. If your test is abnormal, you may be asked to take another test or to have further investigations such as colonoscopy.

question: What are bowel polyps?
answer: Bowel polyps are small growths on the inner lining of the large intestine or rectum that may affect approximately 25 percent of people aged 50 or over.

question: Do bowel polyps cause any symptoms?
answer: Bowel polyps do not usually cause any symptoms, and most people with polyps will not know they have them.

question: How are bowel polyps usually discovered?
answer: Bowel polyps are often discovered during screening for bowel cancer or when the bowel is being looked at for another reason.

question: Who is more likely to develop bowel polyps?
answer: People who have a family member with bowel polyps or bowel cancer, people with conditions like colitis or Crohn's disease, people who are overweight or smoke may be more likely to develop bowel polyps.

question: What are some symptoms of larger bowel polyps?
answer: Some larger polyps can cause constipation or diarrhea, rectal bleeding, pain in your abdomen or a small amount of slime in your poo.

question: What are the treatments for bowel polyps?
answer: The most common procedure for treating bowel polyps is a colonoscopy, where a wire loop is used to burn off or cut off the polyp. Rarely, surgery may be needed to remove part of the bowel. After removal, the polyp is sent to a specialist for analysis.

question: Why is it important to get bowel polyps treated?
answer: If left untreated, some types of polyps (called adenomas) may become cancerous, and most bowel cancers develop from adenoma polyps. Doctors recommend that polyps be treated because of the risk of them developing into cancer.

question: How likely are polyps to turn into cancer?
answer: Only a few polyps will turn into cancer, and it takes many years for this to happen. But, if adenoma polyps are not removed, there is a chance they may eventually become cancerous.

question: How can bowel polyps be monitored?
answer: Based on the diagnosis, the doctor may recommend further testing in 1 to 3 years for people with a certain type of polyp that may be at risk of recurring.

question: What causes bowel polyps?
answer: The exact cause of bowel polyps is not known, but they are thought to be caused by the body producing too many cells in the lining of the bowel.

question: What is brain death?
answer: Brain death is when someone on life support no longer has any brain function, which means they cannot regain consciousness or breathe without support. It is legally confirmed that the person is dead, and there is no chance of recovery.

question: Can brain death be caused by a stroke?
answer: Yes, brain death can be caused by a stroke if the blood supply to the brain is blocked or interrupted, which can also lead to irreversible brain damage.

question: What is the difference between brain death and a vegetative state?
answer: The difference between brain death and a vegetative state is that brain death is permanent and cannot be recovered from, while a vegetative state is a disorder of consciousness that may be recovered from. Someone in a vegetative state may be awake but show no signs of awareness, while someone who is brain dead has no chance of regaining consciousness or breathing without support.

question: What causes brain death?
answer: Brain death can be caused by a number of factors, including cardiac arrest, a heart attack, a stroke, a blood clot, a severe head injury, a brain haemorrhage or other infections, such as encephalitis.

question: What is the role of the brain stem in the brain's core functions?
answer: The brain stem plays an important role in the brain's core functions, such as consciousness, awareness, and movement, by relaying information to and from the brain to the rest of the body and regulating most of the body's automatic functions that are essential for life.

question: How is organ donation related to brain death?
answer: After brain death, it may be possible for the person's organs to be used in transplants, which can often save the lives of others. However, deciding whether to donate their organs can be a difficult decision for partners and relatives.

question: What makes it appear as though someone is brain dead?
answer: A few things can make it appear as though someone is brain dead, including drug overdoses (particularly from barbiturates) and severe hypothermia.

question: Is brain death reversible?
answer: No, brain death is irreversible, according to UK law, and confirmed as legal death. There is no chance of recovery because the body is unable to survive without artificial life support.

question: What is a brain tumour?
answer: A brain tumour is a growth of cells in the brain that multiplies in an abnormal, uncontrollable way.

question: What are the symptoms of a brain tumour?
answer: The symptoms of a brain tumour vary depending on the exact part of the brain affected. Common symptoms include headaches, seizures, persistently feeling sick, mental or behavioural changes, progressive weakness or paralysis on one side of the body, and vision or speech problems.

question: What are the two main types of brain tumours?
answer: The two main types of brain tumours are non-cancerous (benign) brain tumours and cancerous (malignant) brain tumours.

question: What are the grades of brain tumours?
answer: Brain tumours are graded according to how fast they grow and how likely they are to grow back after treatment. Grade 1 and 2 tumours are low grade, and grade 3 and 4 tumours are high grade.

question: What should I do if I have symptoms of a brain tumour?
answer: See a GP if you have symptoms of a brain tumour, particularly if you have a headache that feels different from the type of headache you usually get, or if headaches are getting worse. If the GP cannot identify a more likely cause of your symptoms, they may refer you to a doctor who specialises in the brain and nervous system for further assessment and tests.

question: What are the risk factors for developing a brain tumour?
answer: Risk factors for developing a brain tumour include age, radiation exposure, and family history and genetic conditions.

question: How are brain tumours treated?
answer: Treatment for brain tumours depends on the type of tumour, where it is in your brain, how big it is and how far it's spread, how abnormal the cells are, and your overall health and fitness. Treatments may include steroids, medicines to help with symptoms, surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy.

question: What is the outlook for brain tumour patients?
answer: The outlook for brain tumour patients depends on several factors, including age, the type of tumour they have, where it is in their brain, how effective the treatment is, and their general health. Survival rates are difficult to predict because brain tumours are uncommon and there are many different types. Generally, around 15 out of every 100 people with a cancerous brain tumour will survive for 10 years or more after being diagnosed.

question: Can non-cancerous brain tumours be successfully treated?
answer: Treatment for non-cancerous brain tumours is often successful and a full recovery is possible. Sometimes there's a small chance the tumour could return, so patients may need regular follow-up appointments to monitor this.

question: Who is affected by brain tumours?
answer: Brain tumours can affect people of any age, including children, although they tend to be more common in older adults. More than 11,000 people are diagnosed with a primary brain tumour in the UK each year, of which about half are cancerous. Many others are diagnosed with a secondary brain tumour.

question: What is a breast abscess?
answer: A breast abscess is a painful build-up of pus in the breast caused by an infection. It mainly affects women who are breastfeeding.

question: What are the symptoms of breast abscess?
answer: The symptoms of breast abscess include a painful, red, and warm breast, a lump or swelling in your breast, a high temperature, and feeling generally unwell.

question: What should I do if I am experiencing symptoms of a breast abscess?
answer: You should see a GP if you are experiencing symptoms of a breast abscess. These symptoms include a painful, red and warm breast, a lump or swelling in your breast. A GP will refer you to hospital for treatment if they think you have a breast abscess.

question: Can breast abscess occur in women who are not breastfeeding?
answer: Yes, breast abscess can occur in women who are not breastfeeding but it is less common. Breast abscesses can form if you have a breast infection (called mastitis).

question: What is mastitis?
answer: Mastitis is a type of breast infection that can lead to a breast abscess. It is most often seen in breastfeeding women.

question: What happens during the treatment of a breast abscess?
answer: During the treatment of a breast abscess, an ultrasound scan of your breast will be taken to check for an abscess. The pus can be drained from an abscess with either a needle or a small cut in the skin. Your skin will be numbed before this is done. You can usually go home the same day and may be given antibiotics to take at home.

question: What should I do if my symptoms do not improve within 2 days of starting antibiotics?
answer: You should go back to the GP if your symptoms do not start to improve within 2 days of starting antibiotics.

question: Can I breastfeed during treatment of a breast abscess?
answer: Yes, you can continue feeding with both breasts if you can. This will not harm your baby and can help your breast heal. Try expressing milk from your breasts with your hand or a breast pump if breastfeeding is too painful.

question: What are the causes of a breast abscess?
answer: A breast abscess can form if you have a breast infection (called mastitis) and it's not treated quickly. Mastitis most often affects breastfeeding women.

question: How long does it take for a breast abscess to heal?
answer: The abscess should heal completely in a few days or weeks, depending on the severity of the infection. However, it is important to seek treatment as soon as possible to reduce the risk of complications.
